Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — How do I learn it?
English: How do I learn it?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — How do I learn it?
English: Take one verse at a time, listening and repeating rather than reading. The Practice screen has all seven with a recording against each, and a repeat button. Play a line, say it with the reciter, and move on when it holds. Most people need days, not minutes.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — How do I learn it?
English: Until you have it, say what you know and keep going. No one expects a first-week Muslim to have memorised it, and the prayer you pray while learning is still a prayer.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What am I actually saying?
English: What am I actually saying?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What am I actually saying?
English: It opens by praising God as the Lord of everything and the source of mercy, then turns and speaks to Him directly: You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. The rest is a request: guide us along the straight path. It is a prayer for guidance, said before anything else is asked for.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What is Al-Fatihah?
English: What is Al-Fatihah?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What is Al-Fatihah?
English: The opening chapter of the Qur’an, seven short verses. Its name means "The Opening". It is the most repeated passage in the world: every Muslim says it in every unit of every prayer, which for most people is seventeen times a day.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — Why does every prayer need it?
English: Why does every prayer need it?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — Why does every prayer need it?
English: Because without it there is no prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever does not recite Al-Fatihah in their prayer, their prayer is invalid. Of everything a new Muslim could memorise, this is the one that changes what they are able to do today.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Know what you are saying
English: Know what you are saying

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Know what you are saying
English: Becoming Muslim is one sentence, said and meant. Before you say it, be clear on both halves: that worship belongs to Allah alone and nothing shares that with Him, and that Muhammad ﷺ was sent by Him to convey how.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Know what you are saying
English: It has to be meant. Saying the words to please someone else, or to marry, does not make a person Muslim.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: Say it

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: Say it aloud, in Arabic if you can manage it. If the Arabic is beyond you today, say it in your own language and mean it, then learn the Arabic, because you will say it in every prayer for the rest of your life.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: You are Muslim from the moment you say it and mean it. Nobody has to be there, and no imam has to be present.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: Getting it written down is a separate question, and worth doing when you can. A mosque or Islamic centre can record it and give you a certificate. Not because your Islam needs one, but because other people's paperwork sometimes does.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English:
These are two different things. Whether you are Muslim is settled between you and Allah the moment you say it and mean it, and both answers cited here say so plainly, one of them in the words "Islam is a matter that is between a person and his Lord". Whether a registrar, a mosque, a Hajj visa office or a marriage contract will take your word for it later is a paperwork question with a paperwork answer.

Historically, witnesses were asked for in Muslim courts because inheritance and marriage law followed a person's religion, and that is where the idea that they are required comes from. If you are not ready to walk into a mosque, that is fine. None of this expires, and the certificate is available whenever you want it.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — You are Muslim
English: You are Muslim

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — You are Muslim
English: That is it. Nothing else is required of you in this moment, and nothing you did before it is held against you. Becoming Muslim wipes what came before.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — You are Muslim
English: You do not need to change your name. You do not need to tell anyone today. Take a full wash when you can, which is recommended for someone who has just become Muslim, and then learn wudu and the prayer, in that order, without rushing.

Where it appears: Building consistency — Is a small habit really worth more than a big effort?
English: Is a small habit really worth more than a big effort?

Where it appears: Building consistency — Is a small habit really worth more than a big effort?
English: Yes, and that is not a consolation prize. ʿĀʾishah was asked which deed the Prophet ﷺ loved most and said the one kept up regularly. In his own words, the most beloved deed to Allah is the most regular and constant, even if it is little. Nobody is asked to become a different person in a month. What is asked is to keep the thing you took on.

Where it appears: Building consistency — What do I actually start with?
English: What do I actually start with?

Where it appears: Building consistency — What do I actually start with?
English:
The five prayers. They are the spine, they are obligatory, and everything else hangs off them. Get those to the point where a day without them feels wrong before you add anything. Then one thing: a dua on waking, a short surah after Al-Fatihah, the siwak before prayer. Keep it until you no longer have to remember it. Then one more.

The Prophet ﷺ told people to take on what they could keep up, because Allah does not tire of rewarding until you tire of doing.

Where it appears: Building consistency — What do I actually start with?
English: The page on the small sunnahs lists the little habits and which to take first.

Where it appears: Building consistency — What do I do on a bad week?
English: What do I do on a bad week?

Where it appears: Building consistency — What do I do on a bad week?
English: Shrink it. Do not skip it. A prayer with only Al-Fatihah is a prayer. One line of dhikr instead of the morning list is still the habit, kept. What ends a practice is not the small version. It is the zero, because the zero teaches you that you are someone who does not do this any more. The Prophet ﷺ said the religion is easy, and that whoever makes it hard on himself will not keep it up.

Where it appears: Building consistency — What do I do on a bad week?
English: On the worst days the least is the right amount, and the page on praying before you know everything says what the least is.

Where it appears: Building consistency — What if I already dropped it?
English: What if I already dropped it?

Where it appears: Building consistency — What if I already dropped it?
English: Then pick it up today, smaller than before. A month missed does not undo the months before it, and coming back is not starting from nothing. The page on stopping for a while says the rest, and it is written for exactly this.

Where it appears: Building consistency — Why do people burn out in the first month?
English: Why do people burn out in the first month?

Where it appears: Building consistency — Why do people burn out in the first month?
English: Because the first month is when everything arrives at once. Five prayers, a new way of washing, new words, new food, a mosque, and forty duas you have just found out exist. Taking all of it on in week one, keeping it for three weeks, and dropping most of it in week four is the most common shape of a convert’s first year, and it ends with a person deciding they are bad at being Muslim. They are not. They tried to carry the whole religion up the stairs in one trip.

Where it appears: Clothing — Is this only about women?
English: Is this only about women?

Where it appears: Clothing — Is this only about women?
English: The instruction to lower the gaze and guard modesty is given to men first and then to women, in consecutive verses. That order is worth noticing: modesty in Islam is not a set of rules aimed only at women, and men have their own covering to observe.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for men?
English: What does it mean for men?

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for men?
English: Cover at least from the navel to the knee, keep clothing loose enough not to be revealing, and avoid pure silk and gold jewellery, which the Prophet ﷺ restricted for men. In ordinary Western dress this changes very little in practice.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: What does it mean for women?

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The Qur’an instructs believing women to guard their modesty, to draw their head-coverings over the chest, and to draw their outer garments about them. The commonly taught result is loose clothing covering the body, with the head covered, in front of men outside the immediate family.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: Whether the face and hands must also be covered is a long-standing point of scholarly difference, not a settled question.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: Reference works do not agree on which side is the majority. Dorar’s Encyclopedia of Fiqh calls covering the face the view of most scholars, while summaries written from inside the Hanafi and Maliki schools present the opposite as the common position. So the schools are named below rather than counted. You will meet Muslims on both sides, each following scholarship they trust. The detail of any one school is worth hearing from someone qualified rather than reading in a summary.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The face and hands are what ordinarily shows, so covering them is not required in itself, though the school still calls for covering where there is a real fear of harassment.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The face is not itself among the parts that must be covered, but the position recorded in the school from early on is that it is covered in front of men a woman could marry, because of the harm of not doing so.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The school carries two positions, and the more predominant of them is that the face is covered in front of men a woman could marry.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The position the school takes as most correct is that the face and hands are covered in front of men a woman could marry.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: No one has the right to pressure you, and most people start gradually. If covering would put you in danger, or reveal your conversion before you are ready, that is a real circumstance to discuss with someone knowledgeable, not a rule you are breaking.

Where it appears: Clothing — What is the idea behind it?
English: What is the idea behind it?

Where it appears: Clothing — What is the idea behind it?
English: The Qur’an speaks about clothing as something given for covering and for adornment: both, not one at the expense of the other. Islam is not against looking good. The instructions that follow are about modesty in public, not about drabness.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Add a short surah; ʿAsr — Add a short surah; Tahajjud — Add a short surah; Qiyam al-Layl — Add a short surah; Witr — Add a short surah; Istikhara — Add a short surah; The prayer of repentance — Add a short surah
English: After Al-Fatihah, recite another short surah quietly. Al-Ikhlas is four verses and is where most people start:

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Dhuhr.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Final sitting; ʿAsr — Final sitting; Maghrib — Final sitting; ʿIsha — Final sitting
English: Say the takbir and sit again. This time slide your left foot across under you to the right and sit on the ground, right foot still upright. Rest your left hand on your left knee and your right hand on your right thigh, raise your right index finger, and say:

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Recite Al-Fatihah; ʿAsr — Recite Al-Fatihah; Maghrib — Recite Al-Fatihah; ʿIsha — Recite Al-Fatihah; Tahajjud — Recite Al-Fatihah; Qiyam al-Layl — Recite Al-Fatihah; Witr — Recite Al-Fatihah; Istikhara — Recite Al-Fatihah; The prayer of repentance — Recite Al-Fatihah
English: Recite the opening chapter of the Qur’an quietly, so only you can hear it.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Sit for tashahhud; ʿAsr — Sit for tashahhud; Maghrib — Sit for tashahhud; ʿIsha — Sit for tashahhud
English: Sit for tashahhud

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Stand for the fourth rakʿah; ʿAsr — Stand for the fourth rakʿah; ʿIsha — Stand for the fourth rakʿah
English: Stand for the fourth rakʿah

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Stand for the third rakʿah; ʿAsr — Stand for the third rakʿah; Maghrib — Stand for the third rakʿah; ʿIsha — Stand for the third rakʿah
English: Stand for the third rakʿah

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Stand for the third rakʿah; ʿAsr — Stand for the third rakʿah; Maghrib — Stand for the third rakʿah; ʿIsha — Stand for the third rakʿah
English: Rise to standing, saying the takbir and raising your hands to shoulder level as you rise, then rest your right hand over your left forearm again.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Turn to your left
English: That is Dhuhr complete.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What are the four before and after?
English: What are the four before and after?

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What are the four before and after?
English: Dhuhr has the most voluntary rakʿahs attached to it of the five: four before it and more after. The Prophet ﷺ tied keeping them to a promise no other sunnah prayer carries in the same words.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What if I am at work?
English: What if I am at work?

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What if I am at work?
English: Dhuhr is four silent rakʿahs, a few minutes in any clean, quiet corner. If the window closes on you anyway, the page on missing a prayer walks through catching it up.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What is Dhuhr?
English: What is Dhuhr?

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What is Dhuhr?
English: Four rakʿahs, prayed once the sun has passed its highest point. It is the first prayer of the working day, prayed silently, and one of the five the Prophet ﷺ compared to a river at your door.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — Do I have to take a new name?
English: Do I have to take a new name?

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — Do I have to take a new name?
English:
Becoming Muslim does not require a new name. Most names are simply names, and a name that means something ordinary in another language is not a problem to be solved. Plenty of Muslims you will meet have the name they were born with.

Some people do choose one, and that is theirs to choose. It is a preference, not a step.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — So why do people think you must?
English: So why do people think you must?

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — So why do people think you must?
English: Because the Prophet ﷺ did change some people’s names, where a name carried a meaning worth leaving behind. What is worth noticing is how one of those went. He suggested that a man called Ḥazn, which means something like grief, be called Sahl instead, meaning ease. The man said he would not change the name his father gave him, and he kept it.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — So why do people think you must?
English: That narration is in Bukhari and it is not presented as disobedience. It is the reason to be careful with anybody who tells you this is required.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — What about my family name?
English: What about my family name?

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — What about my family name?
English: This part is not a preference. The Qur’an instructs that people be called by their fathers’ names, and converts keep their family name for the same reason. Your lineage is not something Islam asks you to drop. Cutting yourself off from it is the opposite of what is asked.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — What if I want one anyway?
English: What if I want one anyway?

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — What if I want one anyway?
English: Then take one, and there is no ceremony involved. You do not need permission, a witness, or a legal change, and nothing about your becoming Muslim depends on it. Many people use one among Muslim friends and their own everywhere else, which is not a contradiction.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — What if I want one anyway?
English: If somebody at a mosque starts calling you by a name you did not choose, you are allowed to say you prefer your own.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — Then is it wrong to pray where people can see me?
English: Then is it wrong to pray where people can see me?

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — Then is it wrong to pray where people can see me?
English: No, and this is the question converts actually have, rather than the one this topic is usually written about. Praying at work, fasting in front of colleagues, saying you cannot drink: all of that is visible, and none of it is riyāʾ, because you would be doing it in an empty room too. Riyāʾ is not having an audience. It is the audience being the reason.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — Then is it wrong to pray where people can see me?
English: Much of the obligatory worship is public by design. The prayer is in congregation, zakat is collected, hajj is a crowd. A religion that treated being seen as the problem could not ask for any of it.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — What does this look like for me now?
English: The first year has an unusual amount of announcing in it: telling family, telling friends, being asked about it constantly. Saying what you now believe is not riyāʾ. It is answering a question. The place to watch is smaller and quieter: praying longer because somebody is in the room, or mentioning a fast that nobody asked about. Those are small enough that no one else would ever notice, and that is exactly why they are the ones to watch.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — What if the thought comes in the middle?
English: What if the thought comes in the middle?

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — What if the thought comes in the middle?
English: It will. You are halfway through a prayer and notice that someone is watching, and that part of you is glad. Noticing the thought is not the same as acting on it. The thought arriving is what Shayṭān does, and being annoyed by it is a sign that the intention is alive, not gone. Carry on with the prayer. Do not abandon a good deed because the thought showed up in it. That hands the whole thing over for the price of a distraction.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — What is riyāʾ?
English: What is riyāʾ?

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — What is riyāʾ?
English: Doing an act of worship so that people see you doing it. The narration is blunt about what happens next: whoever makes his deed heard of, Allah will make him heard of, and whoever does it to be seen, Allah will show him up. You asked to be looked at, and you will be. That is the whole payment.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — Why is it treated so seriously?
English: Why is it treated so seriously?

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — Why is it treated so seriously?
English: Because of what it does to the deed itself. In a hadith qudsi, Allah says that of all partners He is the one least in need of a partner: whoever does a deed and associates someone else with Him in it, He leaves him and the one he associated. The deed is not reduced. It is handed over to the person you did it for.

Where it appears: Dua and dhikr — What is dhikr?
English: What is dhikr?

Where it appears: Dua and dhikr — What is dhikr?
English: Dhikr means remembrance: short phrases repeated through the day. Subḥāna-llāh (glory be to God), al-ḥamdu li-llāh (all praise is God’s), Allāhu akbar (God is greatest). The Qur’an says hearts find rest in the remembrance of God, and that describes what it does better than any explanation.

Where it appears: Dua and dhikr — What is dua?
English: What is dua?

Where it appears: Dua and dhikr — What is dua?
English: Dua is simply asking God for something. It has no set form, no required language and no appointed time. The Qur’an says He is near and answers the one who calls. You can make dua in English, in your own words, in the car, and it is the same dua.

Where it appears: Dua and dhikr — What is dua?
English: You do not need Arabic for this. The memorised duas are worth learning because they are the Prophet’s ﷺ wording, not because your own words would be rejected.

Where it appears: Dua and dhikr — Where do I start?
English: Where do I start?

Where it appears: Dua and dhikr — Where do I start?
English: Pick one phrase and one moment, such as waking up or the walk to work. The Dua tab has short ones with the Arabic, how it sounds, and what it means. The shortest is a single word. Starting there is not a compromise.

Where it appears: Dua and dhikr — Why does it matter so much?
English: The Prophet ﷺ compared the person who remembers their Lord to the living, and the one who does not to the dead. He also said that whoever says subḥāna-llāhi wa bi-ḥamdih a hundred times in a day has their sins forgiven though they were like the foam of the sea.

Where it appears: Eid — What do people do before it?
English: What do people do before it?

Where it appears: Eid — What do people do before it?
English: They wash, put on the best clothes they own, and go. On Eid al-Fitr the Prophet ﷺ would eat something before leaving, a few dates. That is worth knowing, because on a festival morning after a month of fasting you might assume you were meant to fast. You are not. Fasting on the two Eids is not done.

Where it appears: Eid — What if I have nobody to spend it with?
English: What if I have nobody to spend it with?

Where it appears: Eid — What if I have nobody to spend it with?
English:
For a lot of converts this is the hardest day of the year, and it is better said plainly than left for you to discover. A family day is a hard day to have no family in.

Go to the prayer. Mosques are at their most welcoming that morning, and somebody will almost certainly invite you to eat. If no one does, it is fine to tell someone there that it is your first Eid. That usually ends with you at a table.

Where it appears: Eid — What if I have nobody to spend it with?
English: Plan it a few days ahead rather than on the morning. An Eid arranged in advance is a very different day from one improvised at 9am.

Where it appears: Eid — What is Eid?
English: What is Eid?

Where it appears: Eid — What is Eid?
English:
There are two, and only two. **Eid al-Fitr** is the morning after Ramadan ends. **Eid al-Adha** falls about ten weeks later, during the days of Hajj. Both begin with a prayer shortly after sunrise, and the rest of the day is food and family.

They are not solemn. People wear their best clothes, children get money, and the mosque is fuller than you have ever seen it.

Where it appears: Eid — What is the Eid prayer like?
English: What is the Eid prayer like?

Where it appears: Eid — What is the Eid prayer like?
English:
Short, and unlike the daily prayers in two ways. It is two rakʿahs with several extra **Allāhu akbar** said before the recitation, and the talk comes after the prayer rather than before it. There is no adhan and no iqamah.

If you do not know when the extra takbirs come, watch the row in front and raise your hands when they do.

Where it appears: Eid — When exactly is it?
English: When exactly is it?

Where it appears: Eid — When exactly is it?
English: Ask your local mosque, and ask a day or two before. The month begins when the new moon is sighted, so the date is not settled until it is, and mosques in the same city sometimes differ by a day. This app does not give you the date, because a calculated date is wrong often enough to matter here.

Where it appears: Eid — When exactly is it?
English: If two mosques near you announce different days, that is an old and ordinary disagreement. Follow the one you pray with.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Are manners really part of it?
English: Are manners really part of it?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Are manners really part of it?
English: Character sits at the centre rather than the edge. The Prophet ﷺ, described in the Qur’an as being of great character, taught that the best of people are those with the best manners, and the people who lived with him said he never used foul or crude language.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Is there a summary?
English: Is there a summary?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Is there a summary?
English: The Prophet ﷺ tied belief directly to behaviour: whoever believes in God and the Last Day should not harm their neighbour, should be generous to their guest, and should say something good or stay quiet. Neighbours, guests, and how you speak. That is a large share of daily life.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What about talking about people?
English: What about talking about people?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What about talking about people?
English: The Qur’an forbids mocking others, assuming the worst, spying, and talking about people behind their backs, in two consecutive verses. Backbiting is treated as a serious wrong, not a small one, and it is the habit most people find hardest to drop.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What do I do when I am angry?
English: What do I do when I am angry?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What do I do when I am angry?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said the strong person is not the one who overpowers others, but the one who controls himself when angry. It is a redefinition rather than a rule, and it comes up more often than most of the rules do.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What is the measure of it?
English: What is the measure of it?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What is the measure of it?
English: One of the shortest things the Prophet ﷺ said and one of the hardest: none of you truly believes until he wants for his brother what he wants for himself. It is the test to apply when a situation is not covered by anything you have learned yet.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What is the measure of it?
English: You will get things wrong, in front of people, for a while. Everyone did. Being embarrassed about it is not a sign you are doing badly.

Where it appears: Fajr — Add a short surah; Dhuhr — Add a short surah; ʿAsr — Add a short surah; Maghrib — Add a short surah; ʿIsha — Add a short surah; Tahajjud — Add a short surah; Qiyam al-Layl — Add a short surah; Witr — Add a short surah; Istikhara — Add a short surah; The prayer of repentance — Add a short surah
English: Add a short surah

Where it appears: Fajr — Add a short surah; Dhuhr — Add a short surah; ʿAsr — Add a short surah; Maghrib — Add a short surah; ʿIsha — Add a short surah; Tahajjud — Add a short surah; Qiyam al-Layl — Add a short surah; Witr — Add a short surah; Istikhara — Add a short surah; The prayer of repentance — Add a short surah
English: This part is sunnah, not required. A prayer of Al-Fatihah alone is a complete prayer, so if you do not know one yet, carry on to the bow.

Where it appears: Fajr — Add a short surah; Maghrib — Add a short surah; ʿIsha — Add a short surah
English: After Al-Fatihah, recite another short surah aloud. Al-Ikhlas is four verses and is where most people start:

Where it appears: Fajr — Bow; Dhuhr — Bow; ʿAsr — Bow; Maghrib — Bow; ʿIsha — Bow; Tahajjud — Bow; Qiyam al-Layl — Bow; Witr — Bow; Istikhara — Bow; The prayer of repentance — Bow
English: Bow

Where it appears: Fajr — Bow; Dhuhr — Bow; ʿAsr — Bow; Maghrib — Bow; ʿIsha — Bow; Tahajjud — Bow; Qiyam al-Layl — Bow; Witr — Bow; Istikhara — Bow; The prayer of repentance — Bow
English: Raise your hands again as you say the takbir, then bow with a straight back, hands gripping your knees, eyes down. Once settled, say:

Where it appears: Fajr — Bow; Dhuhr — Bow; ʿAsr — Bow; Maghrib — Bow; ʿIsha — Bow; Tahajjud — Bow; Qiyam al-Layl — Bow; Witr — Bow; Istikhara — Bow; The prayer of repentance — Bow
English: Settle in each position before you move to the next. This is the thing the Prophet ﷺ sent a man back to repeat his prayer for, three times over.

Where it appears: Fajr — Bow; Dhuhr — Bow; ʿAsr — Bow; Maghrib — Bow; ʿIsha — Bow; Tahajjud — Bow; Qiyam al-Layl — Bow; Witr — Bow; Istikhara — Bow; The prayer of repentance — Bow
English: He told him: bow until you are at rest bowing, then rise until you are standing straight, then prostrate until you are at rest prostrating, then sit until you are at rest sitting, and do that through the whole prayer. Speed is the most common fault in a new Muslim's prayer and the easiest to fix.

Where it appears: Fajr — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Fajr.

English:
What Sahih al-Bukhari establishes is only that the right hand goes over the left forearm. The narration names no place on the body, and Ibn Qudamah records the folding itself as agreed by the majority. After that everyone is reading indirect evidence.

The report naming the chest that Ibn `Uthaymin calls the best on the question is Wa'il ibn Hujr's, and he judges the chest the most correct view even though the well-known position of his own school is below the navel. The narration usually quoted for below the navel, from `Ali, is graded weak by an-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar. Set against that, none of the four schools' well-known positions puts a man's hands on the chest itself.

So the honest summary is that no position here rests on an agreed, authentic, explicit narration, and that is exactly why the schools differ. Follow whichever you are taught locally. No one holds that the prayer fails over it.

Where it appears: Family — Do I have to tell them?
English: There is no requirement to announce it, and no deadline. Some people tell everyone the same week; others wait months, or years, because the cost at home would be serious. Nothing in your prayer or your standing with God depends on who knows.

Where it appears: Family — Do I have to tell them?
English: If it is not safe to tell your family, that is a real situation many converts are in and not a failure of courage. Find one person who knows before you tell anyone who might react badly.

Where it appears: Family — What about marriage?
English: What about marriage?

Where it appears: Family — What about marriage?
English: The Qur’an describes marriage as a place of tranquillity, affection and mercy. That is the standard being aimed at. The Prophet ﷺ said the best of you is the best to his family, and he said it about himself first.

Where it appears: Family — What about marriage?
English: Who you may marry, and what a valid marriage requires, has real detail to it and depends on your circumstances. It is a question to take to someone locally rather than settle from a page.

Where it appears: Family — What if my parents are not Muslim?
English: What if my parents are not Muslim?

Where it appears: Family — What if my parents are not Muslim?
English: This changes nothing about how you treat them. The Qur’an addresses exactly this: even where parents press their child to abandon belief in God alone, the instruction is not to obey them in that, and in the same breath to keep their company in this world with kindness. Both halves are the instruction.

Where it appears: Family — What if my parents are not Muslim?
English: Becoming Muslim does not cancel a family. Converts are sometimes told to distance themselves from non-Muslim relatives; that is not what the text says.

Where it appears: Family — Where do parents sit?
English: Where do parents sit?

Where it appears: Family — Where do parents sit?
English: The Qur’an places kindness to parents immediately after worshipping God alone, in the same sentence. When a man asked the Prophet ﷺ who most deserved his good company, the answer was "your mother", three times, before "your father".

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — Do I have to do any of this?
English: Do I have to do any of this?

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — Do I have to do any of this?
English: No. Ramadan is the fast that is required. Everything on this page is voluntary, and skipping all of it is not a shortcoming. ʿĀʾishah described the Prophet ﷺ fasting in stretches where you would think he would never stop, and then not fasting in stretches where you would think he would never fast again. That is worth holding on to if you have decided you are failing at something.

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — How is it different from Ramadan?
English: How is it different from Ramadan?

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — How is it different from Ramadan?
English: It is not different. The fast itself is the same, dawn to sunset, and it begins with the same intention. What differs is that you can stop. A voluntary fast can be broken partway through without owing anything, which is not true of Ramadan, and that alone makes it a reasonable thing to try on a working day.

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — How should I start?
English: How should I start?

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — How should I start?
English:
One Monday. Not a schedule, not a commitment, not a fast you have announced. Do one, see what it is like on a normal day with a normal job, and decide afterwards.

If it goes badly, that is information rather than failure, and nothing about it is recorded anywhere.

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — How should I start?
English: Do not start the week you also start praying five times. One new thing at a time is how either of them lasts.

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — Which days do people fast?
English: Which days do people fast?

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — Which days do people fast?
English: A few, and they are ordinary rather than obscure. The easiest to start with are the weekly ones, because they need no calendar at all.

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — Which days do people fast?
English: This app does not give the date of ʿAshuraʾ or ʿArafah. Those depend on the moon being sighted, and a calculated date is wrong often enough to be worth not trusting. Ask your mosque in the week beforehand.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Is breaking the fast alone still Ramadan?
English: Is breaking the fast alone still Ramadan?

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Is breaking the fast alone still Ramadan?
English:
An iftar for one, a date, a glass of water and a plate you made yourself in a quiet kitchen, is a full iftar, seen by the One you kept the fast for. The dua for breaking the fast is in the Dua tab, and the moment is yours either way.

It is still worth saying that this is the loneliest recurring moment of a Ramadan kept alone, and it does not have to stay that way.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Is it supposed to feel this strange?
English: Is it supposed to feel this strange?

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Is it supposed to feel this strange?
English:
Ramadan is built as a shared month: shared pre-dawn meals, shared sunsets, whole cities changing rhythm. Keeping it alone, in a place running at its ordinary pace, is genuinely harder than keeping it among people who are also hungry. If your first Ramadan feels like swimming against a current, that is the situation, not a fault in your fasting.

The fast itself is exactly as valid alone as it would be in Mecca. Other people taking part is not a condition of yours.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — What do I say at work or school?
English: What do I say at work or school?

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — What do I say at work or school?
English:
You owe no one an announcement, and you are hiding nothing shameful. Both are true at once, and you choose where you stand between them. Many people simply decline lunch with “I’m good, thanks.” Saying “I’m fasting, it’s Ramadan” is also a complete answer, and most colleagues respond with curiosity rather than hostility.

The questions that follow are nearly always the same three. Not even water? No, not even water. The whole month? Daylight hours, every day. Isn’t that dangerous? Hundreds of millions of people do it every year, and the sick, the pregnant and the travelling are exempt.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — What do I say at work or school?
English: If people at work or at home do not know you are Muslim, you do not have to tell them in order to fast. A quiet “I’m not eating right now” has covered many first Ramadans. The Family page has more on telling people.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — What if someone gives me a hard time?
English: What if someone gives me a hard time?

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — What if someone gives me a hard time?
English: The Prophet ﷺ gave an instruction for exactly this moment, and it is short. The fast is a shield, and if someone picks a fight or insults you while you are keeping it, you say “I am fasting” and leave it there. Out loud or under your breath, either way. The point is that the fast changes how you answer provocation, not only what you eat.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Where are all the other Muslims, then?
English: Where are all the other Muslims, then?

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Where are all the other Muslims, then?
English:
At the mosque, every single evening. Ramadan is the one month of the year when a mosque runs a free communal meal at sunset, open to whoever walks in. Turning up alone is completely unremarkable, because half the room came alone. No one will ask why you are there. If anyone asks anything, it will be whether you have eaten.

If there is a month to make a mosque yours, it is this one. The night prayers afterwards are covered on the page about standing at night, and you can leave whenever you need to.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Where are all the other Muslims, then?
English: Iftar time at the mosque follows the local sighting and the local minute, not this app’s calculation. When they differ, eat when the mosque eats.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Fasting in Ramadan
English: Fasting in Ramadan

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Fasting in Ramadan
English: No food, drink or intimacy from dawn until sunset, for the month of Ramadan.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Fasting in Ramadan
English: Ramadan moves through the year, so its length and difficulty change with the season. There are real exemptions for illness, travel, pregnancy, nursing, menstruation and old age, and taking one is not a failure. Some days are made up later, some are not.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Obligatory charity
English: Obligatory charity

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Obligatory charity
English: A yearly share of the wealth you have held onto, given to those entitled to it.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Obligatory charity
English: Zakat is not a donation you choose to make. It is a portion of your savings that stops being yours. It applies only above a threshold, and only to wealth you have held for a full lunar year, so many people newly earning owe none at all. The app can work out the sum for cash, gold and silver. It counts nothing else, and whether zakat applies to you is still worth asking someone locally.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Pilgrimage
English: Pilgrimage

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Pilgrimage
English: The pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime, for those able to make it.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Pilgrimage
English: Hajj happens on fixed days of the Islamic year and is required once, and only if you can afford it and are physically able. Most Muslims go later in life, if at all. Nothing about it is expected of you now.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Prayer
English: Prayer

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Prayer
English: Five prayers a day, at set times, facing the Kaʿbah in Mecca.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Prayer
English: Fajr before sunrise, Dhuhr after midday, ʿAsr in the afternoon, Maghrib just after sunset, and ʿIsha at night. Each one takes a few minutes. You wash first, which is wudu, and the app walks you through both.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — The testimony of faith
English: The testimony of faith

Where it appears: Five Pillars — The testimony of faith
English: Saying, and meaning, that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His Messenger.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — The testimony of faith
English: This is the pillar the other four rest on. Saying it sincerely is what makes a person Muslim, and it is repeated in every prayer for the rest of your life. It is two statements held together: that worship belongs to Allah alone, and that Muhammad ﷺ is the one who conveyed how.

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: Is supermarket meat halal?

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: People genuinely differ, and you will be told opposite things with equal confidence. The Qur’an permits the food of the People of the Book; what scholars disagree about is whether modern industrial slaughter still resembles what that verse describes. Certified halal meat satisfies every position, which is where most converts start.

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: Muslims in Western countries genuinely differ on supermarket meat, and you will be told opposite things with equal confidence.

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English:
The starting point is not in dispute. All four schools hold that meat slaughtered by Jews and Christians is lawful, and all four hold that an animal killed by strangling, electrocution or anything other than cutting the throat was not lawfully slaughtered at all. What people disagree about is whether a modern slaughterhouse still meets that second condition. Stunning, mechanical blades and who is actually doing the slaughtering are all part of it.

So this is a question about how agreed rules apply today, not a split between the schools, and no school is named here. Some scholars hold that the verse still covers ordinary supermarket meat. Others hold that industrial slaughter no longer resembles what the verse describes, and restrict meat to what is certified. Certified halal meat satisfies every position, which is why most converts start there and settle the question later. Taking the cautious route while you learn is not strange, and relying on the verse is not lax. The specifics are worth asking someone locally rather than settling from an article.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What about eating with my family?
English: What about eating with my family?

Where it appears: Food and drink — What about eating with my family?
English: You do not have to stop eating with people who are not Muslim, and you do not have to make a scene. Eat what you can, quietly leave what you cannot, and answer questions if they come. Most families adjust faster when the change is undramatic.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What about eating with my family?
English: Utensils that touched pork, or a shared roasting tin, worry converts far more than they worry most scholars. Wash it and move on.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What changes at the supermarket?
English: What changes at the supermarket?

Where it appears: Food and drink — What changes at the supermarket?
English: Reading labels, for a few weeks. Then it is automatic.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What is actually forbidden?
English: What is actually forbidden?

Where it appears: Food and drink — What is actually forbidden?
English: Five things, and the Qur’an names each of them outright.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Can I talk during the talk?
English: Can I talk during the talk?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Can I talk during the talk?
English: No, and this is the part visitors most often get wrong. The khutbah is listened to in silence. It is not whispered over or scrolled through. The Prophet ﷺ said that even telling the person beside you to be quiet while the imam is speaking counts as idle talk. If somebody asks you something, a shake of the head is enough.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Can I talk during the talk?
English: Put your phone on silent before you sit down, not after the talk starts. Everyone will hear you fumbling for it.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Do I have to go?
English: Do I have to go?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Do I have to go?
English: For men who can get there, yes. It is obligatory, not just recommended, and that is the one thing about Friday to be clear on. Women may attend and are welcome, but it is not required of them. A woman who prays Dhuhr at home on a Friday has done what is asked of her.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Do I have to go?
English: All the schools agree that Jumuʿah is not obligatory for women. Attending is not discouraged either. Plenty of mosques have a full women’s section on a Friday.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Is this an extra prayer?
English: Is this an extra prayer?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Is this an extra prayer?
English:
No. On Friday the midday prayer is prayed differently. Instead of praying Dhuhr on your own, you go to a mosque, listen to a talk, and pray two rakʿahs behind the imam. That takes the place of Dhuhr. It is not added to it.

So if you pray Jumuʿah, you do not pray Dhuhr as well. People new to this often do both. It is not required.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What actually happens?
English: What actually happens?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What actually happens?
English: You arrive, take your shoes off, and pray two short rakʿahs on your own before you sit down. Then the imam gives a talk from the front, usually about twenty minutes long, in two parts with a short pause in between. When it ends, everyone stands and prays two rakʿahs together. Then it is over and people leave.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if I arrive while it is happening?
English: What if I arrive while it is happening?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if I arrive while it is happening?
English:
Come in quietly and sit down where there is room. If you arrive during the talk, do not walk through the rows looking for a better spot. You still pray the two short rakʿahs first, briefly, because the Prophet ﷺ told a man who came in during the khutbah to stand and pray them.

If you arrive after the congregation has already started praying, join the line where you are and follow the imam from wherever he has got to. When he finishes and gives salam, do not leave. Stand back up and pray the rakʿahs you missed on your own. That last part is what completes your prayer.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if I arrive while it is happening?
English: A latecomer draws no attention. Walking across the front of the room in the middle of the talk is the one thing that does.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if it is my first time?
English: What if it is my first time?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if it is my first time?
English: Stand at the back, watch, and copy. No one is examining you, and every person in that room was new to it once. You do not have to speak to anyone or introduce yourself, and you can leave straight afterwards.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if it is my first time?
English: If you would rather see the room before a Friday, go on a quieter day first. The mosque page covers that.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — When should I get there?
English: When should I get there?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — When should I get there?
English: Before the talk begins, which usually means ten or fifteen minutes before the advertised time. Arriving early is encouraged in its own right, and it also saves you walking in front of a seated room. Washing and putting on clean clothes before you go is part of the day.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Intend
English: Intend in your heart that you are washing to lift the state you are in, then say:

Where it appears: Ghusl — Perform wudu
English: Perform wudu

Where it appears: Ghusl — Perform wudu
English: Do a complete wudu as you normally would, including rinsing your mouth and nose. You may leave washing your feet until the very end.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Pour over your head
English: Pour over your head

Where it appears: Ghusl — Pour over your head
English: Pour water over your head three times, working it through your hair until the water reaches the roots and the scalp is wet everywhere.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Pour over your head
English: Long hair does not need undoing for this, but the water has to reach the scalp underneath.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash the rest of you
English: Wash the rest of you

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash the rest of you
English: Pour water over the right side of your body, then the left, until every part of you has been reached: under the arms, behind the ears, between the toes. Nothing may be left dry.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash the rest of you
English: Take off anything water cannot pass, such as a ring or a watch, or move it as you go.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash your feet
English: If you left your feet until now, wash them, and you are finished.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash your feet
English: This ghusl counts as your wudu too. You can pray without repeating it, as long as nothing breaks your wudu afterwards.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash your hands
English: Wash both hands up to the wrists, three times.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash yourself
English: Wash yourself

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash yourself
English: Wash the private parts and anywhere else on the body carrying impurity, using your left hand. Then wash your hands again.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: When you need it

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Ghusl is required after sex, whether or not anything was released, and after any release of semen, including in your sleep. It is required when a period ends, and when bleeding after childbirth ends. Until you have done it, wudu is not enough and prayer is not valid.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: It is also recommended, though not required, before Friday prayer, before the two Eids, and for someone who has just become Muslim.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The thinner, clear fluid that comes with arousal is not the same thing and does not need a ghusl. Wash the part and the clothing it touched, do wudu, and pray.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: `Ali was too shy to ask and sent al-Miqdad to ask for him. The answer was that it requires wudu, not ghusl. The books keep the two fluids carefully apart, and so does this guide.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Whether the wash on becoming Muslim is required or strongly recommended is a point scholars differ on. Doing it settles the question either way, which is why this app simply says to do it.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English:
Two reports carry it. Thumamah ibn Uthal, released from the pillar of the mosque, went to a nearby grove, washed, came back and said the shahada. Bukhari files that under a chapter headed "taking a bath on embracing Islam". And Qays ibn `Asim came intending to accept Islam and was told to wash.

Scholars read the second report differently, some as a command and some as guidance. The reading that makes it recommended is the more common one, and it is held inside the Hanbali school as well: a group of Hanbalis report it from Ahmad himself, and al-Mardawi, whose role in that school was to say which position it settles on, chose it. No one holds that your Islam is incomplete without it, and no one thinks less of you for doing it a week later than the day itself.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The well-known position of the school holds the full wash obligatory on entering Islam.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Hold it recommended, unless something else, such as intimacy beforehand, had already made a ghusl due.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Hold it recommended rather than owed.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The Friday wash is strongly encouraged rather than owed, and all four schools treat it as a sunnah. The narration that settles it says a wudu on Friday is fine and good, and a ghusl is better.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: All four schools hold the Friday ghusl to be a sunnah. The reading of Bukhari 877, "anyone of you attending the Friday prayer should take a bath", as an obligation is held outside them. Tirmidhi records ash-Shafi`i's own argument for the sunnah reading: `Umar was addressing the congregation when `Uthman arrived having only done wudu, and `Umar reproached him without sending him back to wash. Neither of them treated it as a condition, and both knew the instruction. One practical point the schools also agree on: it only counts as the Friday wash if it is done before the prayer.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The Eid wash is a companion's practice more than a narrated command. Ibn `Umar washed on the morning of Eid al-Fitr before setting out, and the practice has been kept ever since.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The narration that says the Prophet ﷺ himself washed on both Eids is graded weak by Darussalam, so the recommendation does not rest on it, and it is labelled as weak here rather than quietly promoted. What the recommendation rests on is Malik's report of Ibn `Umar in the Muwatta.
