Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is Hajj?
English: What is Hajj?

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is Hajj?
English: The pilgrimage to the Kaʿbah in Mecca, in the days of Dhul-Hijjah, the last month of the year. Millions of people arrive in the same week, dress in the plainest clothes, walk the same route, stand together on the plain of ʿArafah through one afternoon, and go home. It is the fifth pillar. The Qur’an calls the Kaʿbah the House, and calls the journey to it a duty owed to Allah.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is the difference, in one line?
English: What is the difference, in one line?

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is the difference, in one line?
English: Hajj is the pilgrimage with the fixed days and the standing at ʿArafah, owed once in a lifetime to anyone who can make it. Umrah is the short form, in any month. You will meet people who have made Umrah several times and Hajj never, and that is ordinary.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is the difference, in one line?
English: Nothing about either is expected of you now. When it becomes possible, go with a group that knows the rites. Nobody learns Hajj from a page, and this app does not try to teach it.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is Umrah?
English: What is Umrah?

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is Umrah?
English: The smaller pilgrimage: the same journey to the same House, without the fixed days and the standing at ʿArafah that make Hajj what it is. It takes a few hours and it can be made in any month. Many people make it in Ramadan, or on the way to or from Hajj itself. The Qur’an names both together, and the Prophet ﷺ said that one Umrah to the next wipes out what lies between them, and that an accepted Hajj has no reward but Paradise.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is Umrah?
English: Whether Umrah is required once in a lifetime, as Hajj is, or only recommended, is a difference between the schools.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is Umrah?
English: Either way it is not expected of you now, and the practical answer is the same: go when you are able, and go with people who know the way.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is Umrah?
English: Recommended, not required.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — What is Umrah?
English: Required once in a lifetime for whoever is able, like Hajj.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — When does it become mine to do?
English: When does it become mine to do?

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — When does it become mine to do?
English: When you are able. The verse says it is owed by whoever can find a way there, and the scholars read that as being physically able to travel, having the money for the journey without leaving debts or dependants unprovided for, and the road being safe. Until those are true, nothing is owed. Most converts go later in life, and that is not neglect. It is the condition not yet being met.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — When does it become mine to do?
English: The details of what counts as able, and who you travel with, are questions to ask before you book, not to settle from a page.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — Why does it matter so much?
English: Because of what it does to the person who goes. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever performs Hajj for Allah’s sake, without intimacy and without sin during it, comes back as he was on the day his mother bore him. People who have been describe the same thing in plainer words: a week in which everything you usually are, your work, your clothes, your country, is set down, and you are one of two million people in white asking to be forgiven.

Where it appears: Hajj and Umrah — Why does it matter so much?; Dua and dhikr — Why does it matter so much?; ʿAsr — Why does it matter so much?
English: Why does it matter so much?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — Do I need permission for ordinary things?
English: Do I need permission for ordinary things?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — Do I need permission for ordinary things?
English: This is the part people get backwards. Things are permitted unless there is a clear reason otherwise, and the Qur’an describes the Prophet’s ﷺ message as making good things lawful rather than piling on prohibitions. You do not need to find permission for ordinary life.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What about things in between?
English: What about things in between?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What about things in between?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are matters that are unclear, which many people do not know about. Someone who stays away from what is doubtful protects their faith and their honour. That middle ground is where most real questions live.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What about things in between?
English: This is guidance for your own choices, not a licence to police anyone else’s. Being cautious about a doubtful thing for yourself is careful; declaring it forbidden for other people is a different act entirely.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What do halal and haram mean?
English: What do halal and haram mean?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What do halal and haram mean?
English: Halal means permitted. Haram means forbidden. They apply to everything, not just food: how you earn money, how you speak about people, what you wear. Most of life is halal and always was; the forbidden list is short.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What if I am not sure?
English: What if I am not sure?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What if I am not sure?
English: Ask someone qualified, and ask about your actual situation rather than the general case, because circumstances change answers. You will also meet Muslims who are certain of opposite answers on the same question. That usually means it is a genuine point of scholarly difference rather than that one of them is lying to you.

Where it appears: How it began — How did it end?
English: How did it end?

Where it appears: How it began — How did it end?
English: Eight years after being driven out he entered Mecca as its conqueror, and the city gave in. He went to the Kaʿbah, where three hundred and sixty idols stood, and struck them down one by one, saying: truth has come and falsehood has vanished. The tribes of Arabia then entered Islam in crowds, and a short chapter of the Qur’an describes it. He died in Medina ten years after arriving there, at sixty-three.

Where it appears: How it began — What changed in Medina?
English: What changed in Medina?

Where it appears: How it began — What changed in Medina?
English: Medina had invited him, and there the persecuted group became a community. He asked the owners of a piece of land its price, they gave it, and a mosque went up on it with him carrying stones beside his companions. The call to prayer, the fast of Ramadan and most of what Muslims do every day took their settled form there. It is also where permission to fight came, in a verse that says why it was given: because they were wronged, and driven from their homes for saying "our Lord is God". Mecca sent armies against the new community more than once.

Where it appears: How it began — What happened in the cave?
English: What happened in the cave?

Where it appears: How it began — What happened in the cave?
English: He had taken to going alone to a cave on a hill outside Mecca, for nights at a time. On one of those nights the angel Jibril, Gabriel, came to him and said "Read". He answered that he could not read. Three times the angel pressed him, and then the first words of the Qur’an were given to him. He went home shaking and asked Khadijah to cover him. She told him God would never disgrace him, because of how he treated people, and she believed him. The five verses printed here are those words.

Where it appears: How it began — Who was he before that night?
English: Who was he before that night?

Where it appears: How it began — Who was he before that night?
English: Muhammad ﷺ was born in Mecca, a trading town in Arabia built around the Kaʿbah, the house Muslims believe Ibrahim, or Abraham, raised with his son Ismail for the worship of one God. By his time the town worshipped many. He lost both parents as a child, and the Qur’an speaks of it to him directly: did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge? He grew up, married Khadijah, and was forty the night the angel came.

Where it appears: How it began — Why did they leave Mecca?
English: Why did they leave Mecca?

Where it appears: How it began — Why did they leave Mecca?
English: For thirteen years he taught in Mecca, and the town’s leaders turned on the small group that followed him. Some crossed the sea to Abyssinia to be safe. Abu Bakr, his closest friend, set out to do the same, and was talked into returning by a chief who said a man who helped the poor and kept his family ties should not be driven out. In the end the leaders plotted to imprison or kill him, and in 622 he and Abu Bakr left for Medina. They hid in a cave on the way while men searched the hill above them. The Qur’an records what he said there: do not grieve, God is with us.

Where it appears: How it began — Why does the calendar start there?
English: Why does the calendar start there?

Where it appears: How it began — Why does the calendar start there?
English: His companions did not count the years from his birth, or from the first revelation, or from his death. They counted from the day he arrived in Medina. So the year in an Islamic date is the number of years since a persecuted group found a place where it could pray. When the date on the calendar page looks strange, that is what it is counting.

Where it appears: How prayer works — How do I actually learn it?
English: How do I actually learn it?

Where it appears: How prayer works — How do I actually learn it?
English:
By praying, with the guide open. Pick the next prayer of the day, follow it step by step on the mat, and let the pattern teach itself. After a week the guide is confirming what your body already knows. No one learns the prayer from a page and then performs it. Everyone learns it by doing it imperfectly first.

And not knowing all of it yet is not a reason to wait. There is a page on exactly that, and it is short.

Where it appears: How prayer works — So what changes between the five?
English: So what changes between the five?

Where it appears: How prayer works — So what changes between the five?
English: Only the count, and whether you hear the recitation:

Where it appears: How prayer works — So what changes between the five?
English: The Every prayer screen keeps this table one tap away, with the sunnah prayers before and after each one. You never need to hold it in your memory.

Where it appears: How prayer works — What holds the rounds together?
English: What holds the rounds together?

Where it appears: How prayer works — What holds the rounds together?
English: Three joints, and the guides walk you through each of them. The prayer opens with Allāhu akbar. In prayers longer than two rakʿahs, you sit briefly for the tashahhud after the second. At the very end you sit again, say the tashahhud, and close by turning your head to each side with the salam. Everything else is the rounds themselves.

Where it appears: How prayer works — What is one rakʿah?
English: What is one rakʿah?

Where it appears: How prayer works — What is one rakʿah?
English: A rakʿah is one round of the prayer’s movements. When the Prophet ﷺ was asked to teach the prayer, what he listed is short, and it is this round:

Where it appears: How prayer works — What is one rakʿah?
English: That is the unit. A four-rakʿah prayer is this, four times. Nothing new appears in round three that was not in round one.

Where it appears: How prayer works — Why do the five prayers look identical?
English: Why do the five prayers look identical?

Where it appears: How prayer works — Why do the five prayers look identical?
English:
Because they are. Every prayer in Islam is the same movements and the same words, repeated a set number of times. Fajr is not one skill and Maghrib another. There is one skill, and it is smaller than the step-by-step guides make it look. Learn it once and you have learned every prayer you will ever pray, including the voluntary ones.

Only two things change from prayer to prayer: how many times round, and whether the Qur’an is recited aloud or quietly.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — I think I got something wrong. Is the prayer gone?
English: I think I got something wrong. Is the prayer gone?

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — I think I got something wrong. Is the prayer gone?
English: Almost certainly not. What you do depends on what it was, and there are only three kinds of thing it could have been: a doubt with nothing behind it, a small part left out, or one of the few things the prayer cannot do without. Most of what beginners notice afterwards is the first kind, and the answer to the first kind is to do nothing at all.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — It keeps happening. What then?
English: It keeps happening. What then?

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — It keeps happening. What then?
English: Then it is the first kind, the doubt with nothing behind it, and the instruction is the same one the page on losing count gives: ignore it and go on. A doubt that returns after every prayer is not information about your prayers. It is a habit of the mind, and it is answered by not feeding it. Pray, finish, and do not audit.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I actually left out a small thing?
English: What if I actually left out a small thing?

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I actually left out a small thing?
English: The first sitting, a takbir, an extra movement, a word in the wrong place: these are fixed by the two prostrations of forgetfulness, and the page on losing count describes them. If you remember while you are still sitting after the salam, make the two prostrations then; the Prophet ﷺ did exactly that when he ended a prayer early, completed it, and prostrated twice afterwards. If you have already got up and walked away, the answer depends on how long it has been, and on the school you follow.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I actually left out a small thing?
English: Whether a prayer that needed the two prostrations and did not get them has to be repeated is a real difference between the schools.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I actually left out a small thing?
English: Both positions are argued from the same narrations. As a beginner, follow whoever taught you, and do not repeat prayers on your own initiative because a stranger said you should.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I actually left out a small thing?
English: The two prostrations are required. A prayer that needed them and did not get them is repeated.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I actually left out a small thing?
English: The two prostrations are recommended. A prayer without them stands.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I missed something the prayer cannot do without?
English: What if I missed something the prayer cannot do without?

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I missed something the prayer cannot do without?
English: A bowing, a prostration, Al-Fatihah, a whole rakʿah. These are the things the Prophet ﷺ listed when he taught the man who had prayed badly, and he sent that man back to pray because they were missing. If you realise while you are still in your place and only a moment has passed, stand and complete what was missed, then make the two prostrations. If it has been a while, pray it again. That is rare, and it is not a disaster: the second prayer is the prayer.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I missed something the prayer cannot do without?
English: How long is “a while” is a question for a person, not a page. If it happens to you, ask once, and then you will know for good.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I only doubt it?
English: What if I only doubt it?

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I only doubt it?
English: Then let it go. If you finished the prayer and only afterwards began to wonder whether you bowed in the third rakʿah, and you have no actual memory of missing it, the prayer stands. The scholars’ rule is that certainty is not undone by doubt: you were certain you prayed, and a doubt that arrived later does not outweigh that. The Prophet ﷺ taught the same thing for doubt during the prayer, to set aside the doubt and build on what you are sure of. Afterwards, what you are sure of is that you prayed.

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I prayed without wudu?
English: What if I prayed without wudu?

Where it appears: I made a mistake and finished praying — What if I prayed without wudu?
English:
Then pray it again, whenever you realise. The Prophet ﷺ said the prayer of someone who has broken wudu is not accepted until they make wudu, and that is true whether you knew at the time or worked it out afterwards. Nobody is blamed for the mistake. The prayer is simply owed.

If what you found afterwards was something on your clothes rather than a broken wudu, the answer is less simple and depends on what it was and whether you could have known. Ask, and do not assume the worst.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — How do I tell them?
English: How do I tell them?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — How do I tell them?
English:
Earlier than feels comfortable, and more plainly than you want to. What damages a relationship here is rarely the conversion itself. It is the six weeks of a partner sensing that something has changed and not being told what.

You do not need all the answers before you talk to them. "This is real for me, I am still working out what it means, and I am not going anywhere" is a complete opening.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — How do I tell them?
English: A partner’s first reaction is often not their settled one. Give the conversation more than one attempt before concluding anything from it.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — Is my situation unusual?
English: Is my situation unusual?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — Is my situation unusual?
English:
No. Most people do not arrive at Islam alone. They arrive with a partner, or a marriage, or children, and often with none of it discussed yet. It is one of the most common situations converts are in, and any imam you speak to will have handled it many times before.

What is uncommon is being told that in advance.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What happens to my marriage?
English: What happens to my marriage?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What happens to my marriage?
English:
It depends on who you both are, and the answer is genuinely different from one couple to the next. That is why there is no single answer here. What you can know now is that "you must divorce" is not the automatic answer people often assume. Anyone who tells you it is, without asking anything about your situation, is not the person to be advising you.

Take it to somebody who will ask questions first: your local imam, or a scholar you can actually speak to.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What happens to my marriage?
English: This is a genuine area of scholarly difference, and the ruling depends on the case. There is no settled single answer. Somebody who gives you one in a sentence has not understood the question.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What if we are together but not married?
English: What if we are together but not married?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What if we are together but not married?
English:
Then the direction you are being pointed in is marriage, and honestly, that will be a conversation rather than an announcement. Some couples marry. Some separate. Some spend a long time somewhere in between while a partner works out what they think.

All three happen, and none of them means you failed at becoming Muslim.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What should I do first?
English: What should I do first?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What should I do first?
English:
Nothing irreversible, and nothing today. If you remember one thing from this page, remember that.

People in exactly your position have ended marriages, left homes and said things to partners they could not take back, on the strength of a forum post or one confident acquaintance. Then they found out the real answer was different. There is no deadline on this. Pray tonight, and let the question take the weeks it takes.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — Who do I actually ask?
English:
A local imam, in person, with the specifics. Not a forum, not a group chat, and not the most confident person at the mosque. This is the kind of question where confidence and knowledge come apart, and a wrong answer can cost a marriage.

If walking into a mosque feels like too much, many mosques have someone whose job is exactly this. Asking at the office rather than after a prayer is entirely normal.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — Who do I actually ask?; Where do Islamic rulings come from? — Who do I actually ask?
English: Who do I actually ask?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Am I still Muslim?
English: Am I still Muslim?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Am I still Muslim?
English:
Yes. Missing prayers, for a week, a month or longer, does not undo your shahada, and you do not say it again to come back. There is no re-entry, no ceremony, and no one to tell.

That is worth reading twice, because believing you have to start again is the most common reason people never come back.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Do I have to tell anyone?
English: Do I have to tell anyone?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Do I have to tell anyone?
English: No. Not a friend, not an imam, not a group chat. There is no confession in Islam and nothing here needs a witness. If you want to tell somebody because carrying it alone is heavy, that is a good reason. But it is your reason, not a requirement.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — How do I actually come back?
English: How do I actually come back?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — How do I actually come back?
English: You pray the next prayer. That is all. Not a plan, not a fresh start on Monday, not catching up on everything first. Just the next one, whenever it is, even if it is in twenty minutes and you do it badly.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — How do I actually come back?
English: If the full prayer feels like too much tonight, this app has a page on praying before you know everything. Use it. A short prayer tonight beats a perfect one you keep postponing.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What about all the prayers I missed?
English: What about all the prayers I missed?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What about all the prayers I missed?
English: They are a separate question from whether you are back, and they are not a debt you have to clear before you are allowed to start. Deal with the next prayer first. The app has a page on missed prayers for when you want to think about the rest, and it will keep.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What about all the prayers I missed?
English: Anybody who tells you to count up months of missed prayers before praying tonight has the order backwards.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What if it happens again?
English: What if it happens again?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What if it happens again?
English: Then you come back again, the same way, and it counts the same. Nothing about this gets used up, and the door does not close a second time any more than it did the first.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What if it happens again?
English: People often stop in a pattern: the same month, the same trigger. Noticing yours is more useful than promising it will not happen again.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Why does it feel so much worse than it is?
English: Why does it feel so much worse than it is?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Why does it feel so much worse than it is?
English:
Because a gap makes people feel like frauds, and feeling like a fraud is much heavier than missing a prayer. Converts get this especially hard. There is often no one who knew you before, so the gap feels like evidence that the whole thing was a phase.

It is not evidence of anything. The Prophet ﷺ said that he himself sought forgiveness and turned back to God more than seventy times a day. Turning back is not the exception in this religion. It is the normal condition of everyone in it.

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — Is anything not allowed inside marriage?
English: Is anything not allowed inside marriage?

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — Is anything not allowed inside marriage?
English: Two things are ruled out plainly. During menstruation, the Qur’an says to keep away until she is pure. And anal intercourse is forbidden; the Prophet ﷺ described the one who does it as cursed. Beyond those, and the daylight hours of a fast, which the Ramadan page covers, the religion does not hand married people a rulebook.

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — Is anything not allowed inside marriage?
English: Both prohibitions are held across the schools. What is permitted short of intercourse during menstruation, and when it is judged to have ended, have detail to them, and the page on periods and a person are where those go.

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — Is intimacy something Islam is against?
English: Is intimacy something Islam is against?

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — Is intimacy something Islam is against?
English: No. Inside marriage it is wanted, and it is counted for you. The Qur’an says Allah made spouses for each other so that they find rest in one another, and placed affection and mercy between them. Elsewhere it calls husband and wife a garment for each other, which is closeness, warmth and cover all at once. When the companions worried that the rich had taken all the reward by giving charity, the Prophet ﷺ listed what else is charity, and intimacy with one’s spouse was on the list. Nothing about the religion asks you to be ashamed of it.

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — What about the questions this page does not answer?
English: What about the questions this page does not answer?

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — What about the questions this page does not answer?
English: Contraception, a spouse who is not Muslim, what changes during pregnancy, anything medical: these depend on you, and a page cannot hear the part that changes the answer. Ask a person. An imam is used to being asked, and there is nothing embarrassing about a question the scholars have written whole chapters on.

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — What do I do afterwards?
English: What do I do afterwards?

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — What do I do afterwards?
English: The full wash, ghusl, before you next pray. Intercourse makes it due whether or not anything was released, and wudu on its own does not lift the state. If you are going to sleep first, the Prophet ﷺ would wash and make wudu before lying down, and do the ghusl later. There are also words to say beforehand, asking Allah to keep Shayṭān from the two of you and from what He gives you; they are in the dua book.

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — What do I do afterwards?
English: The ghusl guide walks the wash through step by step. It takes a few minutes, and you will do it often enough that it stops being an event.

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — What stays private?
English: What stays private?

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — What stays private?
English: All of it. The Prophet ﷺ said that among the worst of people on the Day of Judgment is the man who goes to his wife, and she to him, and then he tells others what passed between them. That covers friends, family and the internet. If you came from a culture where this is talked about, the silence will feel strange at first. It is a form of respect, and it runs both ways.

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — Where is the line?
English: Where is the line?

Where it appears: Intimacy, modesty and purification — Where is the line?
English: Marriage. The Qur’an praises those who guard their private parts except from their spouses, and there is no third category. Everything the religion says about modesty is there to keep that line easy to hold: lowering the gaze, not being alone with someone you could marry, dressing so that you are not on display. Those are not prudishness. They are the fence around something valued.

Where it appears: Is Allah a different god? — Did the same God send every prophet?
English: Did the same God send every prophet?

Where it appears: Is Allah a different god? — Did the same God send every prophet?
English: Yes. The Qur’an says that no messenger was sent without being told that there is no god but Him. When Jacob was dying and asked his sons what they would worship after him, they answered: your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac, one God. Muslims read that as their own line of descent, in faith if not in blood.

Where it appears: Is Allah a different god? — Did you change gods?
English: Did you change gods?

Where it appears: Is Allah a different god? — Did you change gods?
English: No. The Qur’an gives Muslims the sentence for exactly this conversation. Speaking to Jews and Christians, it tells believers to say: we believe in what was revealed to us and in what was revealed to you, and our God and your God is one. Allah is the Arabic word for God, not the name of a different one. A Muslim believes in the God who spoke to Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and the Qur’an tells believers to say they believe in what was given to every one of the prophets and make no distinction between them.

Where it appears: Is Allah a different god? — So why keep saying "Allah"?
English: So why keep saying "Allah"?

Where it appears: Is Allah a different god? — So why keep saying "Allah"?
English: Because it is the word the Qur’an uses, and the word Muslims share in every language on earth. It has no plural and no feminine form, which suits a God the Qur’an says has nothing like Him. Saying "God" in English is not wrong, and many converts do both. What matters is Who is meant, and He is the same in either word.

Where it appears: Is Allah a different god? — Then what is different?
English: Then what is different?

Where it appears: Is Allah a different god? — Then what is different?
English: What is said about Him. Islam holds that God is one, that nothing was born of Him and He was not born, and that nothing is like Him. Those are the four lines Muslims recite when asked to describe God, and they are the whole of the difference with a Christian who believes God has a son. So a Muslim will say "the same God" and mean it, and will not say "three" or "son", and both things are true at once. It is better to name that than to talk around it.

Where it appears: Is Allah a different god? — Then what is different?
English: If the person asking is Christian, "we pray to the same God, and we differ about Jesus" is a complete answer. The page on Jesus carries the rest, for when they ask.

Where it appears: Is Allah a different god? — What do I actually say?
English: "I haven’t changed gods. Allah is just the Arabic word for God, the same God Abraham and Moses prayed to. Where we differ is what we say about Him, not who He is." You can stop there. If it turns into a debate, the Qur’an gives you the line for the moment: Allah is our Lord and your Lord, for us our deeds and for you yours, there is no argument between us, and God will bring us together.

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — But the Qur’an does tell Muslims to fight?
English: But the Qur’an does tell Muslims to fight?

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — But the Qur’an does tell Muslims to fight?
English: Yes, and it is worth knowing where those verses sit. For the years in Mecca the Muslims were persecuted and did not fight. Permission came after they had been driven from their homes, and the verse that gives it says why: because they were wronged. The limits are in the text itself. Fight those who fight you, and do not go beyond that. If the other side inclines to peace, incline to it. And people who are not fighting you and have not driven you out are to be treated with kindness and justice.

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — But the Qur’an does tell Muslims to fight?
English: A verse about fighting will usually be quoted at you without the lines around it. Ask which verse, and read it in its place.

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — What do I actually say?
English: You do not have to win the argument. Something like this is enough. "Islam counts one life as all of humanity, and the Prophet ﷺ forbade harming women and children. People who do that are breaking the religion, not following it." Then stop. If they want the verses, they are above. If they want to argue about the news, that is a conversation about the news, and you are allowed to say you are new and still learning.

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — What do I actually say?
English: Watch for the question that is really about you: "Are you going to become like that?" It wants reassurance, not a verse. Answer the worry.

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — What do I actually say?; What about Jesus? — What do I actually say?; Is Allah a different god? — What do I actually say?; Was Islam spread by the sword? — What do I actually say?; Why do women cover? — What do I actually say?; Why can’t you eat that? — What do I actually say?
English: What do I actually say?

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — What does the Qur’an say about killing?
English: What does the Qur’an say about killing?

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — What does the Qur’an say about killing?
English: The verse to know says that whoever kills a person, other than for murder or for spreading corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all of humanity. And whoever saves one life, it is as if he had saved all of humanity. Two more verses speak to Muslims directly. Do not kill any person, whom God has made sacred, except by right, meaning with lawful cause and never by private decision. And whoever kills a believer deliberately is promised Hell.

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — What is a Muslim held to?
English: What is a Muslim held to?

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — What is a Muslim held to?
English: Justice, even towards people you have reason to hate. The Qur’an tells believers to stand firm as witnesses for justice, and not to let hatred of a people push them into being unjust. It tells them to answer a bad deed with a better one, so that an enemy becomes a close friend. Hold the news up against that. When someone acting in Islam’s name kills the innocent, the standard has been broken, not followed.

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — Who may never be harmed?
English: Who may never be harmed?

Where it appears: Isn’t Islam violent? — Who may never be harmed?
English: During one of the Prophet’s ﷺ campaigns a woman was found killed, and he forbade the killing of women and children. That instruction is the basis of the rules of war in Islamic law. Fighting is between fighters, and the people not fighting are off limits. Someone who kills civilians in the name of Islam is breaking the instruction of the man he claims to follow.

Where it appears: Istikhara — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Istikhara.

Where it appears: Istikhara — Then ask
English: Then ask

Where it appears: Istikhara — Then ask
English: The prayer is finished. Still sitting, say the dua, and where it says “this matter”, name the thing you are deciding.

Where it appears: Istikhara — Then ask
English: That is Istikhara complete.

Where it appears: Istikhara — What can I ask about?
English: What can I ask about?

Where it appears: Istikhara — What can I ask about?
English: Any time except the times when prayer is held off, and about anything you genuinely have a choice in: a job, a move, a marriage, something smaller. Not about whether to do something already settled as right or wrong; there is nothing to ask about there.

Where it appears: Istikhara — What do I say?
English: What do I say?

Where it appears: Istikhara — What do I say?
English: Said after the two rakʿahs. Where it says “this matter”, name the thing you are deciding.

Where it appears: Istikhara — What is istikhara?
English: What is istikhara?

Where it appears: Istikhara — What is istikhara?
English: Two rakʿahs and a dua, prayed when you have a decision to make. Jabir reported that the Prophet ﷺ taught it for every matter the way he taught a surah of the Qur’an, which tells you how ordinary it was meant to be, and how often.

Where it appears: Istikhara — What sign should I expect?
English: What sign should I expect?

Where it appears: Istikhara — What sign should I expect?
English: This is the part people are told wrong. The dua asks God, if the thing is good for you, to bring it about and make it easy, and if it is bad for you, to turn it away and turn you away from it. It does not promise a sign, a dream or a feeling. You pray, and then you decide, and what follows is the answer.

Where it appears: Istikhara — What sign should I expect?
English: You still have to think, ask people who know, and weigh it up. Istikhara goes alongside that, not instead of it.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — I have lost count. What now?
English: I have lost count. What now?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — I have lost count. What now?
English: If you cannot remember whether you are on the second or third rakʿah, assume the smaller one, the number you are certain of, and carry on from there.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — I have lost count. What now?
English: Do not start the prayer again. Restarting is the common instinct and it is not the answer.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — It keeps happening. Is that bad?
English: It keeps happening. Is that bad?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — It keeps happening. Is that bad?
English: Everyone loses count, including people who have prayed all their lives. If the doubt keeps coming back in the same prayer, ignore it and finish. Chasing certainty is itself a distraction from the prayer.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What are the two extra prostrations?
English: What are the two extra prostrations?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What are the two extra prostrations?
English: Finish the prayer as normal. Before or after the final taslim, make two prostrations just as you do in the prayer itself, saying the takbir as you go down and as you come up, then give the taslim.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What are the two extra prostrations?
English: Schools differ on whether these come before or after the taslim. Either is taught by scholars; do it the way whoever taught you does it.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What else does that fix cover?
English: What else does that fix cover?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What else does that fix cover?
English: Those two prostrations also cover forgetting the first sitting, adding a movement by mistake, or saying something in the wrong place.

Where it appears: Maghrib — Does it have to be right at sunset?
English: Does it have to be right at sunset?

Where it appears: Maghrib — Does it have to be right at sunset?
English: Its window runs until ʿIsha, but it is the shortest window of the five. That is why Maghrib is the prayer most often prayed the moment it comes in.

Where it appears: Maghrib — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Maghrib.

Where it appears: Maghrib — Turn to your left
English: That is Maghrib complete.

Where it appears: Maghrib — What is Maghrib?
English: What is Maghrib?

Where it appears: Maghrib — What is Maghrib?
English: Three rakʿahs, prayed as the light goes. It is the only one of the five with an odd count, and the first prayer recited aloud since dawn.

Where it appears: Maghrib — What is prayed after it?
English: What is prayed after it?

Where it appears: Maghrib — What is prayed after it?
English: Two quiet rakʿahs, part of the twelve daily voluntary rakʿahs the Prophet ﷺ tied to a house built in Paradise.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — So how do people actually meet?
English: So how do people actually meet?

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — So how do people actually meet?
English:
Openly, and with somebody else around. There is no dating in the sense of a private relationship that may or may not turn into something. The assumption is that you are talking because you are considering marriage, and that you are not doing it alone.

In practice that means meeting through family, through a mosque, or through an app made for it, and then meeting in public or with somebody present. This is the part converts most often get wrong, usually by accident, and usually by carrying over what they already knew.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What am I meant to be looking for?
English: What am I meant to be looking for?

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What am I meant to be looking for?
English: The Prophet ﷺ listed the four things people marry for, wealth, family standing, beauty and religion, and said to choose for religion. That is not a demand for austerity. It is a ranking, and religion is the only one of the four that survives everything else changing.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What are the pieces called?
English: What are the pieces called?

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What are the pieces called?
English: Four words that will come up constantly, and are never explained to a newcomer.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What are the pieces called?
English: What a walī is for, and what happens when a convert woman has no Muslim family, is a real question the schools answer differently. It is one to take to somebody local rather than settle from a page.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What if I am already married?
English: What if I am already married?

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What if I am already married?
English: Then this page is not about your situation. Becoming Muslim while married is common, and it has its own answer, which depends on who your spouse is and what happens next. It has its own page, and this one would give you the wrong picture entirely.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What if I am already married?
English: Do not act on anything about an existing marriage from general reading. It is the single most common place converts are given bad advice by well-meaning strangers.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What is a Muslim marriage?
English: What is a Muslim marriage?

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What is a Muslim marriage?
English:
A contract, agreed in front of witnesses. It is not a sacrament and not a religious mystery. It is an offer, an acceptance, a gift from the husband to the wife, and people present who heard it. It can happen in a living room in ten minutes.

Most of what you will see at a wedding, the venue, the clothes, the several hundred guests, is culture on top of that. None of it is the marriage.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — I missed a prayer. Is that a sin?
English: I missed a prayer. Is that a sin?

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — I missed a prayer. Is that a sin?
English: Sleeping through a prayer or forgetting it is not a sin. You pray it as soon as you wake or remember, and that prayer counts as the one you missed.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if I missed several?
English: What if I missed several?

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if I missed several?
English: Missed more than one? Pray them in the order they were due, then the prayer you are currently in time for.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if it keeps happening?
English: What if it keeps happening?

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if it keeps happening?
English: What ends people’s prayer is not the prayer they missed. It is deciding that they are now the sort of person who misses prayers. Pray the next one, and you are back.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if it keeps happening?
English: Deliberately leaving a prayer is a serious matter and different from oversleeping. The action is still the same: pray it, and pray the next one.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — Is everything I read a rule?
English: Is everything I read a rule?

Where it appears: Must, should, may — Is everything I read a rule?
English:
Read about Islam for a week and you will meet dozens of sentences that sound like instructions. They are not all the same kind of instruction, and if you read them all as commands you will end the month exhausted and convinced you are failing at everything.

There are five categories. Learning them once is the difference between a religion with a shape and a religion that is one long list.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What are the five?
English: What are the five?

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What are the five?
English: From the strongest to the strongest against, with everything ordinary in the middle.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What does it mean when this app says “should”?
English: What does it mean when this app says “should”?

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What does it mean when this app says “should”?
English: It usually means mustaḥabb: worth doing, not required. Where something is genuinely obligatory, the app says so plainly, and where the schools of thought differ it says that too. You are not expected to take all of it on at once, and nothing here is keeping score.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What does it mean when this app says “should”?
English: Take the obligatory things first and let the rest arrive slowly. That is the order everybody learns them in.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What if nobody has told me either way?
English: What if nobody has told me either way?

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What if nobody has told me either way?
English: The starting position is that a thing is permitted unless there is a reason it is not. That is why the forbidden list is short and nameable, and why nobody can hand you a new prohibition without showing you where it comes from.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What if nobody has told me either way?
English: A useful question when somebody tells you something is haram: which of the five, and on what basis? It is a fair question and it is not rude.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Does patience mean doing nothing?
English: Does patience mean doing nothing?

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Does patience mean doing nothing?
English: Sabr means holding steady: carrying on doing the right thing while something is hard, rather than accepting whatever happens. The Qur’an pairs it with prayer as the two things to seek help through, which is a practical instruction more than a moral one: when it is bad, pray.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — What does gratitude actually mean?
English: What does gratitude actually mean?

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — What does gratitude actually mean?
English: The Qur’an says that if you are grateful, He will increase you. Much of gratitude in practice is simply naming things, which is why al-ḥamdu li-llāh is said constantly, over small things, out loud. It is a habit of attention rather than a feeling you wait for.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — What does this look like for me now?
English: The first year often costs something real: family who do not understand, friends who drift, a life that has to be rearranged. That difficulty is not a sign you chose wrongly, and it is exactly the situation the word sabr is for.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Why are these always paired?
English: Why are these always paired?

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Why are these always paired?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said the believer’s situation is remarkable, because everything that happens to them is good: when something pleasant comes they are grateful and that is good for them, and when something painful comes they are patient and that is good for them. Nobody else, he said, is in that position.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Do I still pray?
English: Do I still pray?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Do I still pray?
English: From the moment bleeding starts until it stops, you do not pray. This is not permission to skip. You are not supposed to pray, and praying anyway is not better.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Do I still pray?
English: You do not make these prayers up afterwards. They are not a debt. This surprises most people, so it is worth saying twice: they are simply not owed.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about after giving birth?
English: What about after giving birth?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about after giving birth?
English: Bleeding after childbirth follows the same rules as a period: you do not pray, you do not make those prayers up, and you take a ghusl when it ends.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about fasting?
English: What about fasting?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about fasting?
English: You do not fast during a period. Fasts missed in Ramadan for this reason are made up later, before the next Ramadan, at your own pace.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about fasting?
English: Prayer and fasting work differently here. Prayers are not made up; fasts are.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What can I still do?
English: What can I still do?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What can I still do?
English: Everything else stays open to you. You can make dua in your own words, say dhikr, listen to the Qur’an, go on learning, and sit with people who are praying.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What can I still do?
English: You are not unclean and you are not excluded. The rest from prayer is a concession you have been given, not a punishment or a mark against you.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What if the bleeding is not a period?
English: What if the bleeding is not a period?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What if the bleeding is not a period?
English: Bleeding outside your normal pattern, or lasting far beyond it, is treated differently, and it does not stop you praying. A woman asked the Prophet ﷺ exactly this and was told not to give up her prayers, because that bleeding comes from a blood vessel rather than being a period. You wash, do wudu, and pray; the wudu is done afresh for each prayer.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What if the bleeding is not a period?
English: Telling the two apart is genuinely a question for someone knowledgeable, not for an app. Do not guess, and do not stop praying on a guess.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — When do I start praying again?
English: When do I start praying again?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — When do I start praying again?
English: Once the bleeding has stopped, take a ghusl, the full wash, and you go straight back to praying with the next prayer due.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: Why do people tell me different things?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: One question here is genuinely open and two are not, and it saves a lot of confusion to know which is which. Reciting the Qur’an during a period is the open one: scholars divide on it, and you will meet people certain of opposite answers. Holding a printed muṣḥaf is not open in the same way, because all four schools say not to. Nor is sitting in the prayer hall of a mosque, which all four treat as somewhere not to stay through a period, though several allow walking through.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: None of this touches what the last section said. Listening, dua, dhikr and learning are open on every account, and nobody who tells you one of these is being difficult with you.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: On reciting the Qur’an there is no settled answer, and both sides are held by people who know exactly what they are doing.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: On the muṣḥaf, the agreement is about touching it directly. Scholars treat a barrier between hand and page differently, so if you need to carry one or turn its pages, that is the thing to ask about. On the mosque, the agreement is about staying there. The Shafi`i and Hanbali schools permit passing through, and several contemporary scholars go further. If any of this affects your week, ask someone knowledgeable which position your local mosque follows.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: Permit reciting during a period, which is also al-Shafi`i’s earlier position and one narration from Ahmad.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: The settled positions of the Hanafi, Shafi`i and Hanbali schools hold back from reciting until the period ends.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn `Uthaymin took the permitting view, and it is the verdict of the Permanent Committee.

Where it appears: Phrase: Akhī · Ukhtī
English: My brother · my sister.

Where it appears: Phrase: Akhī · Ukhtī
English: How people will address you, including people who have just met you. It is ordinary, not familiar.

Where it appears: Phrase: Al-ḥamdu li-llāh
English: All praise is for Allah.

Where it appears: Phrase: Al-ḥamdu li-llāh
English: After good news, after eating, after sneezing, and as the normal answer to “how are you?”

Where it appears: Phrase: Allāhu akbar
English: Opens every prayer and every call to it. Also said in ordinary life at anything striking, good or bad, the way subḥāna-llāh is.

Where it appears: Phrase: Allāhu aʿlam
English: Allah knows best.

Where it appears: Phrase: Allāhu aʿlam
English: Ends an answer the speaker is not certain of. Scholars say it after a ruling; everyone says it after a guess. It is a useful thing to be able to say yourself.

Where it appears: Phrase: As-salāmu ʿalaykum
English: Peace be upon you.

Where it appears: Phrase: As-salāmu ʿalaykum
English: The greeting, arriving or passing. Said to you before almost anything else.

Where it appears: Phrase: As-salāmu ʿalaykum
English: Wa ʿalaykumu s-salām, and peace be upon you. Always answer it.

Where it appears: Phrase: Astaghfiru-llāh
English: I seek Allah’s forgiveness.

Where it appears: Phrase: Astaghfiru-llāh
English: Said after a slip, or on hearing something that should not have been said.

Where it appears: Phrase: Bāraka-llāhu fīk
English: May Allah bless you.

Where it appears: Phrase: Bāraka-llāhu fīk
English: Thanks, praise, or simply warmth towards you.

Where it appears: Phrase: Bāraka-llāhu fīk
English: Wa fīka bāraka-llāh, and may He bless you.

Where it appears: Phrase: In shāʾa-llāh
English: If Allah wills.

Where it appears: Phrase: In shāʾa-llāh
English: Attached to anything about the future. Not a soft no, whatever you may have been told. It is an acknowledgement that the future is not ours to promise.

Where it appears: Phrase: Innā li-llāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn
English: To Allah we belong, and to Him we return.

Where it appears: Phrase: Innā li-llāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn
English: On hearing that someone has died, or of a serious loss.

Where it appears: Phrase: Jazāka-llāhu khayran
English: May Allah reward you with good.

Where it appears: Phrase: Jazāka-llāhu khayran
English: Thank you. You will hear this far more often than the Arabic for “thanks”.

Where it appears: Phrase: Jazāka-llāhu khayran
English: Wa iyyāk, and you.

Where it appears: Phrase: Mā shāʾa-llāh
English: What Allah has willed.

Where it appears: Phrase: Mā shāʾa-llāh
English: Admiring something: a child, a new job, good news. Said so that admiration carries no envy with it.

Where it appears: Phrase: Raḍiya-llāhu ʿanhu
English: May Allah be pleased with him.

Where it appears: Phrase: Raḍiya-llāhu ʿanhu
English: Said after the name of one of the Prophet’s companions. “ʿanhā” for a woman.

Where it appears: Phrase: Ṣalla-llāhu ʿalayhi wa sallam
English: May Allah’s prayers and peace be upon him.

Where it appears: Phrase: Ṣalla-llāhu ʿalayhi wa sallam
English: Said after the Prophet’s name. Written as ﷺ, and that single character is this whole phrase.

Where it appears: Phrase: Subḥāna-llāh
English: Glory be to Allah.

Where it appears: Phrase: Subḥāna-llāh
English: Astonishment, at something beautiful or something terrible.

Where it appears: Phrase: Taqabbala-llāhu minnā wa minkum
English: May Allah accept it from us and from you.

Where it appears: Phrase: Taqabbala-llāhu minnā wa minkum
English: Around Eid and after Ramadan, about the worship of the month just gone.

Where it appears: Phrase: ʿĪd Mubārak
English: A blessed Eid.

Where it appears: Phrase: ʿĪd Mubārak
English: On either of the two Eids.

Where it appears: Phrase: ʿĪd Mubārak
English: Say it back.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Do I still recite?
English: Do I still recite?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Do I still recite?
English: In the prayers recited aloud, Fajr, Maghrib and ʿIsha, the imam recites and you listen. In the silent ones you recite quietly to yourself as usual. Either way, you say the same things in bowing and prostration that you would say alone.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Do I still recite?
English: Whether you also read Al-Fatihah quietly behind the imam in a prayer recited aloud is a point on which the schools genuinely differ. Follow what the mosque you are in does.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What am I actually meant to do?
English: What am I actually meant to do?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What am I actually meant to do?
English:
Follow the imam, and follow him slightly late. The Prophet ﷺ said the imam is appointed to be followed, so you bow once he has bowed, not with him and never before him. If you find yourself moving at the same moment as him, you are going too early.

That is most of it. The prayer is the same prayer you already know. What changes is that somebody else decides when each movement happens.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What if I join late?
English: What if I join late?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What if I join late?
English: Join wherever they are, in the row where there is space, and follow from there. When the imam gives salam, stand back up and pray the rakʿahs you missed on your own. That last part is what completes your prayer, and it is the part people forget.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What if I lose track?
English: What if I lose track?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What if I lose track?
English: Keep following. You do not have to know which rakʿah it is. The imam does, and your job is to be in the same position as him. If everyone sits and you were about to stand, sit. No one is watching you the way it feels.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What if I lose track?
English: If the imam makes a mistake, men say **subḥān Allāh** and women clap once. You will hear it happen. It is normal, and it is not a scandal.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Where do I stand?
English: Where do I stand?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Where do I stand?
English: In the row, shoulder to shoulder, filling the gaps. Rows are straightened before the prayer starts, and somebody may touch your shoulder or foot to line you up. That is not a correction aimed at you. It happens to everyone. If a row is full, start the next one behind it.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Where do I stand?
English: Do not stand alone behind a full row if there is space in it. Step in; people will make room.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Will anyone notice I am new?
English: Will anyone notice I am new?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Will anyone notice I am new?
English: Less than you think. A room in prayer is looking forward, not sideways. Stand at the back, copy the person next to you, and accept that you will be half a second behind everything. Half a second behind is exactly where you are meant to be.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — Does it count the same?
English: Does it count the same?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — Does it count the same?
English: A prayer prayed sitting because you could not stand is not worth less than one prayed standing. It is the prayer you were asked for.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — How do I bow and prostrate?
English: How do I bow and prostrate?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — How do I bow and prostrate?
English: Lean forward a little for the bowing, and further forward for the prostration, so that the prostration is clearly lower than the bow. Say everything exactly as you would standing.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot sit either?
English: What if I cannot sit either?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot sit either?
English: Pray lying on your right side facing the qibla, or on your back, and make the movements with your head or your eyes. Prayer is never dropped for illness while you are conscious.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot stand?
English: What if I cannot stand?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot stand?
English: If standing is beyond you, or would cause real pain or harm, pray sitting down, on a chair or on the floor, whichever you can manage.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — Can I pray two together?
English: Can I pray two together?

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — Can I pray two together?
English: You may also pray Dhuhr and ʿAsr together, and Maghrib and ʿIsha together, at the time of either one of the pair.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: How far counts as travelling?

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: Far enough that you would ordinarily call it travelling. There is no distance in the Qur’an or in any narration, so scholars have had to draw the line themselves, and they draw it in different places. The most common answer works out at somewhere around eighty to ninety kilometres. What everyone agrees on is when it starts: not when you decide to go, but once you have actually left the place you live.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: A daily commute is not a journey, however long it feels. If you are unsure, ask someone locally rather than deciding alone.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: No verse and no narration gives a distance. The figure most scholars use is a conversion of a classical measure, and a second position holds there is no fixed distance at all: if it is a journey, you may shorten.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English:
A barid is a classical measure of distance, and four of them is two days of travel by loaded camel. Converted into modern units it lands near eighty-eight kilometres, and different conversions give slightly different numbers, which is most of why you will hear eighty from one person and ninety from another.

How long you may keep shortening once you arrive is a second difference. The Maliki and Shafi`i schools stop at four days, the Hanafi school at fifteen, and some hold that there is no limit while you have not settled.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: The Maliki, Shafi`i and Hanbali schools put it at four burud, which converts to roughly eighty-eight kilometres.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: Reckon it from a journey of about three days at the pace people travelled then, which the school gives as forty-eight miles, or roughly seventy-seven kilometres.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn `Uthaymin held there is no fixed distance: anything ordinarily called travelling counts.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How much do I pray when travelling?
English: How much do I pray when travelling?

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How much do I pray when travelling?
English: On a journey, the four-rakʿah prayers, Dhuhr, ʿAsr and ʿIsha, are prayed as two. Fajr stays two and Maghrib stays three.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How much do I pray when travelling?
English: This is a gift, not a compromise. It is the practice of the Prophet ﷺ on journeys, not a lowering of the bar.

Where it appears: Qadr — It still sits badly with me. Is that a problem?
English: It still sits badly with me. Is that a problem?

Where it appears: Qadr — It still sits badly with me. Is that a problem?
English: No. The six articles page says the same and it bears repeating: this is the article the scholars wrote the most about, precisely because it is hard, and finding it hard is not a sign your faith is faulty. You are not asked to solve how knowledge and choice fit together. You are asked to hold both ends, act as if your choices matter, because they do, and rest on the fact that the outcome was known, because it was. People have argued the middle for fourteen centuries. Nobody has ever needed to win that argument in order to pray.

Where it appears: Qadr — So are my choices real?
English: So are my choices real?

Where it appears: Qadr — So are my choices real?
English:
Yes, and the Qur’an would make no sense otherwise. It says: whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve. It says the soul was given both its wickedness and its righteousness, and that the one who purifies it succeeds and the one who corrupts it fails. A book that commands, forbids, praises and blames is talking to people who can choose.

What the Qur’an rejects is using decree as an excuse. It puts the words “if Allah had willed, we would not have done it” in the mouths of those who associated others with Him, and answers that people before them said the same. You cannot sin and blame the register.

Where it appears: Qadr — Then what is the belief for?
English: Then what is the belief for?

Where it appears: Qadr — Then what is the belief for?
English:
Steadiness. The verse that says every disaster was written first goes on to say why you are told: so that you do not despair over what has passed you by, and do not gloat over what you were given. The Prophet ﷺ taught a boy riding behind him the same thing in a sentence: if the whole of creation gathered to benefit you, they could only do what Allah had already written for you, and if they gathered to harm you, the same.

Held rightly, that is not a cage. It is the reason you can lose a job, or a person, or a year, and not conclude that you did everything wrong. Some of the outcome was never yours.

Where it appears: Qadr — What do I do with it day to day?
English: What do I do with it day to day?

Where it appears: Qadr — What do I do with it day to day?
English:
Try hard, and then let go of the result. The Prophet ﷺ said a strong believer is better and more loved by Allah than a weak one, and told people to go after what benefits them, ask Allah’s help, and not lose heart. Then he said what to do when it goes wrong anyway: do not say “if only I had done otherwise”, because that door opens onto regret with no floor. Say instead that Allah decreed it, and what He willed He did.

A man asked whether he should tie his camel and trust Allah, or leave it loose and trust Allah. Tie it, he was told, and trust. That is the whole practice in four words.

Where it appears: Qadr — What do I do with it day to day?
English: Applied for a job: prepare properly, then whatever comes was written. Someone you love is ill: get them the best care you can, then whatever comes was written. Both halves, every time.

Where it appears: Qadr — What does divine decree mean?
English: What does divine decree mean?

Where it appears: Qadr — What does divine decree mean?
English: That nothing takes Allah by surprise. Before anything happens, He knew it, it was written, He willed that it come to be, and He created it. The Qur’an says that no disaster strikes on earth or in yourselves except that it is in a register before it is brought into being, and that everything was created with measure. That is the belief in full. It is a statement about Allah, not a theory about you.

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Qiyam al-Layl.

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — How do I finish?
English: How do I finish?

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — How do I finish?
English: Whatever you pray at night, end it with witr, a single rakʿah that makes the night’s total odd. It is what closes the night prayer.

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — How is it different from tahajjud?
English: How is it different from tahajjud?

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — How is it different from tahajjud?
English: Whether you slept. Pray at night before sleeping and it is qiyam al-layl; sleep first, wake, and pray, and that is tahajjud. Both are voluntary, both are the same movements, and nobody is doing the lesser one.

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — How is it different from tahajjud?
English: This is the whole difference. If you are unsure which you prayed, it does not affect whether it counted.

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — Turn to your left
English: That is Qiyam al-Layl complete.

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — What is qiyam al-layl?
English: What is qiyam al-layl?

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — What is qiyam al-layl?
English: Praying at night, before you have slept. Any amount, any part of the night after Isha. It is the same prayer you already know: two rakʿahs at a time, as many times as you want.

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — Where will I hear the word?
English: Where will I hear the word?

Where it appears: Qiyam al-Layl — Where will I hear the word?
English: In Ramadan, mosques announce “qiyam” for the long night prayers in the last ten nights. Taraweeh is the same family of prayer. You are welcome at it, you can leave when you need to, and nobody is counting your rakʿahs.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What are suhoor and iftar?
English: What are suhoor and iftar?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What are suhoor and iftar?
English: Suhoor is the meal before dawn. The Prophet ﷺ said to take it, because there is blessing in it, and skipping it makes a long day much harder. Iftar is breaking the fast at sunset, traditionally with dates and water, and he taught not to delay it once the sun is down.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What does the fast involve?
English: What does the fast involve?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What does the fast involve?
English: From first light until sunset, no food, no drink, not even water, and no sexual intimacy. The Qur’an marks the start of the fast as the moment dawn becomes distinguishable, and the end at sunset. Outside those hours you eat and drink normally.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: What happens at the end?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: The month ends with Eid: a morning prayer, new or good clothes, and visiting people. Before that prayer, every Muslim gives a small fixed amount of food so that nobody is left out of the day. It is called zakat al-fitr and it is due for every member of a household, old and young, and paid on behalf of anyone in your care.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Whether it may be given as money instead of food is a real difference, and it decides what you actually hand over. Most mosques and charities collect it either way and will tell you which they are doing.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Nothing about your Eid depends on getting this right in your first year. Give it through whoever your local mosque collects for, in the form they ask for, before the Eid prayer. That satisfies the position they follow, and the timing is the part the narration is strictest about.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Allow the value in money, and consider it easier for the recipient.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Malik, ash-Shafi`i and Ahmad hold that it is the staple food the narration names, given as food rather than as its value.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens the rest of the month?
English: What happens the rest of the month?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens the rest of the month?
English: Mosques fill up for taraweeh, a long optional night prayer, and many people read far more Qur’an than usual. Jibril would go through the Qur’an with the Prophet ﷺ each night of Ramadan. There is also more giving: he was described as at his most generous this month.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Laylat al-Qadr?
English: What is Laylat al-Qadr?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Laylat al-Qadr?
English: One night in Ramadan is called Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Decree, the night the Qur’an began to be revealed, which the Qur’an says is better than a thousand months. Nobody is told which night it is. The Prophet ﷺ said to look for it in the odd nights of the last ten, which is why mosques fill up at the end of the month.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Ramadan?
English: What is Ramadan?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Ramadan?
English: The ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, and the month in which the Qur’an began to be revealed. Because the calendar is lunar, it moves about eleven days earlier each year, so it passes through every season over a lifetime.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Who does not have to fast?

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: The Qur’an names two: anyone ill, and anyone travelling. Both make the days up afterwards, at their own pace, before the next Ramadan. It also gives a second route for someone who could only fast with real hardship: feeding a poor person for each day instead of fasting it. That second route is the answer for a long-term or permanent condition, where making the days up later is not something that is ever going to happen. During a period a woman does not fast either, and those days are made up.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: If you are on medication or managing an illness, ask a doctor and someone knowledgeable before your first Ramadan rather than during it. A first Ramadan is far more often damaged by someone fasting who should not have than by someone taking an exemption they were given.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Not fasting when you are exempt is not a failure and not something to feel guilty about. The exemption is part of the instruction, not a loophole in it.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Pregnancy and breastfeeding are the case scholars genuinely divide over. That you may stop fasting where there is real risk to you or the baby is agreed; what you owe afterwards is not, and the answer can turn on whether the worry was for you or for the child.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: There is also a fifth position, older than all four: Ibn `Abbas and Ibn `Umar held that a pregnant or breastfeeding woman feeds a poor person for each day and does not make the days up at all. It is the gentlest of the answers, and it is still taught. Among contemporary scholars, Ibn Baz, Ibn `Uthaymin and the Permanent Committee held that the days are made up. Nothing here needs deciding in the abstract. Work out with someone knowledgeable what applies to your own situation, and do it before Ramadan rather than in the middle of it.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Make the days up, and nothing else is owed.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: A pregnant woman makes the days up. A breastfeeding woman makes them up and also feeds a poor person for each day.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: If she stopped fasting out of fear for herself, she makes the days up. If out of fear for the child alone, she makes them up and feeds a poor person for each day.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: The same distinction as the Shafi`i school.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Feeding a poor person for each missed day is what "fidyah" means when you hear the word. Most mosques and Muslim charities collect it and will tell you the amount they use locally.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Why fast at all?
English: Why fast at all?

Where it appears: Ramadan — Why fast at all?
English: The Qur’an gives the reason directly: so that you may become mindful of God. It is not endurance for its own sake, and it is not a diet. Being hungry at four in the afternoon is a reminder of who provides, and of people for whom that hunger is not a choice.

Where it appears: Reference: Your mother, three times
English: Your mother, three times

Where it appears: Reference: Your mother, three times
English: The answer he ﷺ gave, and then gave again

Where it appears: Reference: Your neighbour
English: Your neighbour

Where it appears: Reference: Your neighbour
English: The one Jibril would not stop mentioning
