Where it appears: Reference: ʿAsr
English: The afternoon prayer, and the weight it carries

Where it appears: Reference: ʿIsha
English: The night prayer, and how the day ends

Where it appears: Sincerity — Does it have to feel sincere?
English: Does it have to feel sincere?

Where it appears: Sincerity — Does it have to feel sincere?
English: No. Sincerity is a direction, not a mood. You point a deed at Allah by deciding, before you start and again when you notice you have drifted, that it is for Him. Some days that decision comes with warmth and some days it is dry, and the dry day counts as much as the other. Waiting to feel sincere before you pray is a way of not praying.

Where it appears: Sincerity — How would I know if I have it?
English: How would I know if I have it?

Where it appears: Sincerity — How would I know if I have it?
English: Ask whether the deed changes when nobody can see it. Longer prayers in company and shorter ones alone, a fast mentioned before anyone asked: those are the signs that somebody else has become part of the reason. The opposite is not hiding your religion. Praying at work is visible and is not showing off, because you would do it in an empty room too. The page on doing it to be seen draws that line carefully, and this page is its other half: what to aim at rather than what to avoid.

Where it appears: Sincerity — What does it look like day to day?
English: Bigger than worship. The Prophet ﷺ told Saʿd that he would be rewarded for whatever he spent for Allah’s sake, even the morsel he put in his wife’s mouth. Feeding your family, going to work, being patient with a parent: all of it can be done for Allah, and when it is, it is worship. Sincerity does not make your life more religious by adding acts to it. It turns the acts you already do towards Him.

Where it appears: Sincerity — What does it look like day to day?
English: A habit worth having: before an ordinary task, one silent sentence saying who it is for. It takes a second, and it changes what the task is.

Where it appears: Sincerity — What makes a deed count?
English: What makes a deed count?

Where it appears: Sincerity — What makes a deed count?
English: What it was for. The first narration in Sahih al-Bukhari, the one students of hadith learn before any other, says that deeds are by their intentions and that every person has what they intended. The example it gives is emigration: the same journey, made for Allah or made for a woman, is two different journeys. The act was identical. The intention was the deed.

Where it appears: Sincerity — Who am I doing this for?
English: Who am I doing this for?

Where it appears: Sincerity — Who am I doing this for?
English: That is the whole question, and Islam asks it before it asks anything else. The Qur’an says people were commanded only to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion, and then to pray and to give. Sincerity comes first in the sentence, before the acts. A prayer, a fast, a kindness, and the same prayer, fast and kindness done so that someone notices, are two different deeds that look identical from outside.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in Allah
English: Belief in Allah

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in Allah
English: That Allah is one, without partner, and that nothing else deserves worship.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in Allah
English: The other five sit inside this one. It is not only accepting that God exists. It is accepting that He is one, that nothing shares His authority, and that worship is owed to Him alone. Everything you say in prayer is a restatement of it.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in divine decree
English: Belief in divine decree

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in divine decree
English: That nothing happens outside Allah’s knowledge and will, the good and the hard alike.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in divine decree
English: This is the one people find hardest, and it is usually misread as meaning your choices do not matter. It does not. You still choose, and you are still answerable for what you choose. Held rightly it settles you rather than paralyses you: you act as well as you can, and you are not crushed by the part of the outcome that was never yours to control.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in divine decree
English: If this one sits badly with you at first, that is normal and it is not a sign your faith is faulty. It is the article scholars have written the most about, precisely because it is difficult.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the angels
English: Belief in the angels

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the angels
English: That Allah created angels, who carry out what He commands.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the angels
English: Angels are created beings. They are not divine, not partners of Allah, and not prayed to. Jibril, who brought the revelation to the Prophet ﷺ, is the one you will hear named most often. You are not asked to picture them or explain them, only to accept that they are real.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the Last Day
English: Belief in the Last Day

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the Last Day
English: That this life ends, everyone is raised, and each person answers for what they did.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the Last Day
English: Nothing you do is lost or goes unweighed, including what nobody else ever saw. When the Day comes is known only to Allah. Working out dates for it is not part of believing in it, and people who claim to have done so are to be ignored.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the messengers
English: Belief in the messengers

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the messengers
English: That Allah sent prophets to every people, and that Muhammad ﷺ is the last of them.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the messengers
English: Many of them will already be familiar: Ibrahim, Musa, ʿIsa, and others shared with Judaism and Christianity. Islam honours them as men Allah sent, not as divine, and does not let you accept some and reject others. Muhammad ﷺ closes the line; no prophet comes after him.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the revealed books
English: Belief in the revealed books

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the revealed books
English: That Allah sent scripture to guide people, and that the Qur’an is the last of it.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the revealed books
English: The Qur’an names earlier revelations, among them the Tawrat given to Musa and the Injil given to ʿIsa. Believing in them means believing Allah sent them. It does not mean the texts other faiths read today are those revelations as they were sent.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Tahajjud.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — How do I actually start?
English: How do I actually start?

Where it appears: Tahajjud — How do I actually start?
English: Set an alarm twenty minutes before Fajr rather than for the middle of the night. You are already going to be awake for Fajr; this is standing up a little earlier. Starting there is why people keep it.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — How little counts?
English: How little counts?

Where it appears: Tahajjud — How little counts?
English: There is no minimum to reach and no number to work up to. Two rakʿahs, on one night, is the thing itself. People who pray it for decades mostly pray a little, often, which is the pattern the Prophet ﷺ described as the deeds God loves most, the small ones kept up.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — How little counts?
English: It is the same prayer you already know. Nothing about the movements or the words changes. Only the time, and that you chose to be there.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — Turn to your left
English: That is Tahajjud complete.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — What if I have not slept?
English: What if I have not slept?

Where it appears: Tahajjud — What if I have not slept?
English: Tahajjud is prayed after waking, which is what separates it from simply staying up late. If you have not slept, you are praying qiyam al-layl, which is also good, also voluntary, and not what this word means.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — What is tahajjud?
English: What is tahajjud?

Where it appears: Tahajjud — What is tahajjud?
English: A prayer in the last part of the night, after you have slept and before Fajr. The Qur’an tells the Prophet ﷺ to keep part of the night for it as something additional, and that word matters: it is not owed. Nobody is behind for not praying it.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Intend
English: Intend in your heart that you are purifying yourself for prayer, in place of using water.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Touch the ground
English: Touch the ground

Where it appears: Tayammum — Touch the ground
English: Place both palms flat on a clean natural surface: earth, sand, stone, or dust settled on something. Lift them and shake off any excess.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Touch the ground
English: It does not have to be soil. A dusty windowsill or a stone wall will do.

Where it appears: Tayammum — When it ends
English: When it ends

Where it appears: Tayammum — When it ends
English: Tayammum breaks for the same reasons wudu breaks, and it ends the moment water becomes available to you.

Where it appears: Tayammum — When you can use it
English: When you can use it

Where it appears: Tayammum — When you can use it
English: Tayammum replaces wudu, and replaces ghusl, when there is no water you can reach, when using it would make you ill or make an illness worse, or when the only water available is needed for drinking.

Where it appears: Tayammum — When you can use it
English: It is not for when water is merely inconvenient. But it is genuinely allowed when it applies, and people miss prayers they were permitted to pray.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your face
English: Wipe your face

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your face
English: Wipe both palms once over your whole face.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: Wipe your hands

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: Wipe the back of your right hand to the wrist with your left palm, then the back of your left hand with your right. You are finished and may pray.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: Some schools wipe the arms to the elbows instead of stopping at the wrists. Both are taught by scholars; you will see people do it either way.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: In the narration the Prophet ﷺ struck the earth once, blew the dust off, and wiped the face and the backs of the hands. The two wordings Bukhari carries put those in either order, which is why you will see both taught. This guide follows the order of the wudu verse: face, then hands. Schools that teach wiping to the elbows argue from other narrations and from that same verse. Nobody will think you have prayed invalidly either way.

Where it appears: The angels — Do I need to picture them?
English: Do I need to picture them?

Where it appears: The angels — Do I need to picture them?
English: No. The Qur’an describes them in a few lines and leaves the rest unsaid, and so should you. What belief in them asks is smaller and more useful than a picture: that you take the recorders seriously, that you know who brought the book you recite from, and that you stop thinking of yourself as unwatched.

Where it appears: The angels — Do I need to picture them?
English: When a mosque feels empty at Fajr, remember the shift change. You are being counted.

Where it appears: The angels — Do Muslims pray to angels?
English: Do Muslims pray to angels?

Where it appears: The angels — Do Muslims pray to angels?
English: No, and the Qur’an rules it out in the same breath as praying to prophets: no messenger sent by Allah would order people to take angels or prophets as lords. They carry nothing to Allah on your behalf. You ask Him, directly, in your own words, and the angels write it down.

Where it appears: The angels — What are angels?
English: What are angels?

Where it appears: The angels — What are angels?
English: Created beings, made from light, who do exactly what Allah tells them and nothing else. The Qur’an says of them that they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, but do what they are ordered. They are not gods, not the souls of the dead, and not a decoration in the story. They are workers, and they are everywhere the work is.

Where it appears: The angels — What do they do around me?
English: What do they do around me?

Where it appears: The angels — What do they do around me?
English:
More than you would guess, and the narrations describe it in ordinary detail. Angels come to you in shifts, by night and by day, and the shifts meet at Fajr and at ʿAsr. The ones who spent the night with you go up and are asked about you, and answer that they left you praying and found you praying. While you sit in the place you prayed, before you move, they ask forgiveness for you.

None of that is a threat. It is the reason an empty room at dawn is not empty, and the reason nothing you do for Allah goes unrecorded, including the things nobody else ever saw.

Where it appears: The angels — Which ones will I hear named?
English: Which ones will I hear named?

Where it appears: The angels — Which ones will I hear named?
English: Four come up constantly, and the Qur’an names or describes each.

Where it appears: The animals and the land — And if you do not?
English: And if you do not?

Where it appears: The animals and the land — And if you do not?
English: The same teaching has a second half, and it is not softened. A woman was punished over a cat she had shut in until it died. She neither fed it nor gave it water, and she did not let it go to feed itself. Nothing in the account says she was cruel beyond that. She simply kept an animal and did not attend to it, which is a thing anyone can do without noticing.

Where it appears: The animals and the land — What about the land itself?
English: What about the land itself?

Where it appears: The animals and the land — What about the land itself?
English: Whoever plants a tree or sows a crop has given charity for every bird, person or animal that eats from it. The reward is not conditional on who eats or on it being meant for them. Against that, the Qur’an describes the man who moves through the land causing corruption and destroying crops and cattle, and says plainly that God does not love corruption.

Where it appears: The animals and the land — What about the land itself?
English: The narration counts what is taken without permission as charity too. A tree is not a transaction.

Where it appears: The animals and the land — What did that look like?
English: What did that look like?

Where it appears: The animals and the land — What did that look like?
English: A man on a journey went down a well to drink, and came up to find a dog panting and eating the earth from thirst. He said that this animal was suffering what he had just suffered. He went back down, filled his shoe with water, carried it up in his teeth and gave the dog a drink. He was forgiven for it. The companions asked whether there was really a reward for them in animals, and the Prophet ﷺ said there is a reward for serving any living thing.

Where it appears: The animals and the land — What is actually owed here?
English: What is actually owed here?

Where it appears: The animals and the land — What is actually owed here?
English: Mercy, and the texts treat it as a disposition rather than a list of rules. The merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful, and the instruction is to be merciful to those on the earth so that the One above the heavens will be merciful to you. The Qur’an gives the reason underneath it. There is no creature on the earth, and no bird that flies, but they are communities like you. They are not scenery, and they are going back to their Lord as you are.

Where it appears: The best of you — Does it run both ways?
English: Does it run both ways?

Where it appears: The best of you — Does it run both ways?
English: Yes. The Qur’an says that what is due to them is like what is due from them, in what is reasonable. The clause sits inside a longer passage about the waiting period after a divorce, which is worth knowing before you look it up, and the principle in it is stated in general terms. A right that only ever runs one way is not what the verse describes.

Where it appears: The best of you — What if the feeling fades?
English: What if the feeling fades?

Where it appears: The best of you — What if the feeling fades?
English: The command does not move. The Qur’an tells husbands to live with them in kindness, and then says something unusually direct about the months when that is hard. You may dislike a thing, and God places much good in it. Kindness is not presented as what you do while the feeling lasts. It is what is owed, and the feeling is expected to come and go under it.

Where it appears: The best of you — What if the feeling fades?
English: Nothing on this page settles a dispute in a marriage. Anything specific needs a person who can hear both sides and ask questions back.

Where it appears: The best of you — What is the measure of a man here?
English: What is the measure of a man here?

Where it appears: The best of you — What is the measure of a man here?
English: His wife. The Prophet ﷺ said that the best of you is the best to his wives, and then said that he was the best of them to his own. That is a standard set at home, where nobody is watching and there is no credit to be had. A man can be admired everywhere else and fail it.

Where it appears: The best of you — Why is marriage framed this way?
English: Why is marriage framed this way?

Where it appears: The best of you — Why is marriage framed this way?
English: Because of what the Qur’an says it is for. It calls a spouse a sign of God, made so that you find rest in them, and says He placed affection and mercy between the two of you. Rest, affection and mercy are the stated purpose. A marriage that runs on none of the three is missing the thing it was described as being.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Am I supposed to say something back?
English: Am I supposed to say something back?

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Am I supposed to say something back?
English: The usual thing is to quietly repeat what the caller says, line by line, while the adhan is being called, and then to say a short dua afterwards. Neither is obligatory, and neither is complicated.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Am I supposed to say something back?
English: If you do not know the words yet, listening is enough. No one starts out knowing them.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Does this mean I am late?
English: Does this mean I am late?

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Does this mean I am late?
English: Hearing the adhan for a prayer you have not prayed yet does not mean you are late. It means that prayer has just become available. The times card on the Today screen shows when each window closes, and that is the part worth knowing.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Does this mean I am late?
English: Mosques call at slightly different minutes from a calculated timetable. If your mosque differs from this app, follow the mosque.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — What am I hearing?
English: What am I hearing?

Where it appears: The call to prayer — What am I hearing?
English:
The adhan is the announcement that a prayer’s time has come in. It is called out from a mosque, from a phone, or sometimes by one person in a room, and it happens five times a day, at the times shown in this app.

It is not a summons you are late for, and it is not a countdown. It marks the opening of a window, and the window is usually hours long.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Why did it happen twice?
English: Why did it happen twice?

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Why did it happen twice?
English: The adhan announces the time. A second, shorter call, the iqamah, is given immediately before a congregation actually starts praying. If you are in a mosque and hear a second call a few minutes after the first, that is people standing up to pray, not a mistake.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: How does this affect my week?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: For most of the year, not at all. You will pick the date up from the people around you and never need to work it out. It only matters at the two ends of Ramadan, and there it is announced locally rather than calculated in advance, so mosques in the same city can start the month, or the Eid, a day apart. That is normal and not worth worrying about.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Whether a month begins by sighting the moon locally or by astronomical calculation is a live question, and communities in the same country sometimes start Ramadan on different days.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Both approaches are argued from evidence, and neither community is being careless. As a beginner, the practical answer is to follow the mosque or community you pray with.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Follow the sighting of the moon, as reported locally or regionally.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Some bodies accept astronomical calculation to fix the date in advance.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the sacred months?
English: What are the sacred months?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the sacred months?
English: The Qur’an says four of the twelve are sacred, and the Prophet ﷺ named them in his farewell sermon: three consecutive ones, Dhul-Qaʿdah, Dhul-Hijjah and Muharram, and Rajab. Fighting is prohibited in them, and wrongdoing in them is treated as more serious.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the twelve months?
English: What are the twelve months?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the twelve months?
English: In order, from the start of the year. Four are sacred, two carry an Eid and one carries the fast. The other five have nothing particular in them. Several are named for a season they no longer fall in, because the months kept moving and the names did not: Rabiʿ means spring, and Jumada is the dry part of the year.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the twelve months?
English: You may hear that Safar is an unlucky month, or that it is a bad time to marry or travel. That is a pre-Islamic superstition, and the Prophet ﷺ named it and rejected it. No month carries bad luck.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Which months ask anything of me?
English: Which months ask anything of me?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Which months ask anything of me?
English: Only one thing in the year is obligatory, and that is Ramadan, which has a page of its own. Four other things are worth knowing about, because you will hear all four mentioned, and none of them is required. The fast of ʿAshuraʾ, on the tenth of Muharram, which the Prophet ﷺ kept and which became voluntary once Ramadan was prescribed. Fasting in Shaʿban, which he did more than in any month except Ramadan. Six fasts spread through Shawwal, after Ramadan. And the first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah, which he described as the best days of the year for doing good.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Why does the date move every year?
English: Why does the date move every year?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Why does the date move every year?
English: Because the year is made of twelve lunar months, each beginning with a new moon, and that makes it about eleven days shorter than the solar year. So Ramadan and the two Eids arrive about eleven days earlier each year rather than falling on fixed dates. Over a lifetime they pass through every season.

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?
English: Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?
English: You are forgiven by turning back to God and meaning it. There is no ceremony and nothing to perform. This prayer is something you may do, not a step you have missed. It exists because doing something with your body often helps when saying it in your head does not.

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?
English: There is no limit, and no shame in praying it often. Somebody who prays it twice in a week has not failed twice. They have turned back twice.

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying The prayer of repentance.

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — Turn to your left
English: That is The prayer of repentance complete.

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — What is it for?
English: What is it for?

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — What is it for?
English: Abu Bakr reported that the Prophet ﷺ said no one does something wrong, then gets up and purifies himself, then prays, then asks God’s forgiveness, except that God forgives him. Wudu, two rakʿahs, and asking. Nothing more is needed.

Where it appears: The prophets — Can I believe in some and not others?
English: Can I believe in some and not others?

Where it appears: The prophets — Can I believe in some and not others?
English: No, and this is the part that surprises people who came from another faith. Believing in the prophets means all of them, as men Allah sent, without ranking one people’s prophet above another’s. The Qur’an puts the words in the believers’ mouths: we make no distinction between any of His messengers. You do not give up Musa or ʿIsa by becoming Muslim. You keep them, and you stop being asked to choose.

Where it appears: The prophets — Did they teach different religions?
English: Did they teach different religions?

Where it appears: The prophets — Did they teach different religions?
English: One religion, in the words each people spoke. The Qur’an says that no messenger was sent before Muhammad ﷺ except that he was told: there is no god but Me, so worship Me. It names Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa and says what was laid on them is what was laid on him: establish the religion, and do not be divided in it. The laws given to each differed in detail. The thing being taught did not.

Where it appears: The prophets — Was there only one line of them?
English: Was there only one line of them?

Where it appears: The prophets — Was there only one line of them?
English: No. The Qur’an says a messenger was sent into every nation, and that no people passed without a warner among them. Most are not named, and you are not asked to know who went to whom. The point is the opposite of exclusivity: nobody, anywhere, was left without someone telling them what you now know.

Where it appears: The prophets — What is a prophet?
English: What is a prophet?

Where it appears: The prophets — What is a prophet?
English: A man Allah chose to carry His message to people, and to show them how to live by it. Not a god, not part-god, not an angel in a body. The Qur’an has the Prophet ﷺ say it himself: I am only a man like you, to whom it has been revealed that your God is one God. What sets a prophet apart is what was given to him, not what he was made of.

Where it appears: The prophets — Which names should I know?
English: Which names should I know?

Where it appears: The prophets — Which names should I know?
English: The ones you will hear most, in the order they came.

Where it appears: The prophets — Which names should I know?
English: Muslims say “peace be upon him” after a prophet’s name, ʿalayhi s-salam, and ﷺ after Muhammad’s. You will hear both constantly, and nobody minds if you forget.

Where it appears: The revealed books — Is that the Bible I grew up with?
English: Is that the Bible I grew up with?

Where it appears: The revealed books — Is that the Bible I grew up with?
English:
Partly, and this is worth saying carefully. Muslims believe the Tawrat and the Injil were sent, exactly as the Qur’an says. What Muslims do not believe is that the books on a shelf today are those revelations word for word as they were given. The Qur’an says plainly that some people wrote scripture with their own hands and then said it was from Allah. So a Muslim honours the revelation to Musa and to ʿIsa without being bound to every line of a modern edition, and without needing to decide which line is which.

If you loved the book you grew up with, nothing here asks you to despise it. Where it agrees with the Qur’an, the Qur’an confirms it. Where the two differ, the Qur’an is the one you follow.

Where it appears: The revealed books — Is that the Bible I grew up with?
English: That the earlier scriptures were sent by Allah is an article of faith. That the texts in circulation are not guaranteed to be those scriptures as sent is the settled Sunni position, and this page states it without going further.

Where it appears: The revealed books — What do I do with this?
English: What do I do with this?

Where it appears: The revealed books — What do I do with this?
English: Read the Qur’an as the book that was sent to you, and treat the earlier ones with respect rather than as rivals. When a relative quotes the Bible at you, you are not obliged to attack it. You can say that Muslims believe Allah sent scripture to Musa and to ʿIsa, that the Qur’an confirms what is true in it, and that you follow the Qur’an where they differ. That is the whole position, and it is a calm one to hold at a table.

Where it appears: The revealed books — What does believing in the books mean?
English: What does believing in the books mean?

Where it appears: The revealed books — What does believing in the books mean?
English: That the Qur’an is not the first time Allah spoke to people, and that the earlier times were real. The Qur’an tells believers to believe in the Book sent down to the Messenger and in the Scripture sent down before him, in one sentence, as one instruction. A Muslim does not think revelation began in the seventh century. It began with the first prophet, and the Qur’an is the last of a line.

Where it appears: The revealed books — What is different about the Qur’an?
English: What is different about the Qur’an?

Where it appears: The revealed books — What is different about the Qur’an?
English: Two things, both stated by the Qur’an about itself. It confirms what came before it and stands as a criterion over it, which is why a Muslim reads the earlier books through it and not the other way round. And it is preserved: Allah says He sent it down and He will guard it. That promise is not made about any other book, and it is why the Arabic you recite in prayer is the same Arabic recited fourteen centuries ago.

Where it appears: The revealed books — What is different about the Qur’an?
English: What the Qur’an is, and how to begin reading it, has its own page and its own tab. This one only says where it sits among the others.

Where it appears: The revealed books — Which books does the Qur’an name?
English: Which books does the Qur’an name?

Where it appears: The revealed books — Which books does the Qur’an name?
English: Five, given to five prophets, in this order.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — How many should I take on?
English: How many should I take on?

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — How many should I take on?
English:
One. Then, once it has stopped being something you remember to do, one more.

The way this goes wrong is a person adopting twelve at once in their first month, keeping none of them past week three, and concluding they are bad at being Muslim. Nothing here is a checklist and nothing is measured. A habit you have held for two years is worth more than eleven you dropped.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What about the little duas?
English: What about the little duas?

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What about the little duas?
English: They are already in this app, in the dua book, in the book’s own wording: waking, leaving the house, entering and leaving the bathroom, before and after eating, entering a mosque. They are not repeated here. In the book they can be searched, pinned, and read in Arabic and English together.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What about the little duas?
English: The dua tab has them grouped by moment. Take one, use it for a fortnight until you stop having to look, and only then take another.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What are they?
English: What are they?

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What are they?
English:
Small habits the Prophet ﷺ kept, which Muslims take on gradually over years. Starting with the right side. Cleaning your teeth. A short dua on waking, on leaving the house, before eating. None of them is required, none is difficult, and together they turn ordinary parts of a day into something deliberate.

They are the part of the religion that is least discussed with converts and most visible in people who have been Muslim a long time.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What is the siwak?
English: What is the siwak?

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What is the siwak?
English:
A twig from the arāk tree, used to clean the teeth. You will see them sold outside mosques for very little. The Prophet ﷺ said that if it were not hard on people, he would have ordered it before every prayer. That tells you how much he valued it, and also that he did not make it a requirement.

A toothbrush does the cleaning. Many people use the siwak as well, before prayer and on Fridays.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — Why do people start with the right?
English: Why do people start with the right?

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — Why do people start with the right?
English:
Because he did. ʿĀʾishah described the Prophet ﷺ as liking to begin with the right side: putting on shoes, combing his hair, washing. It applies to entering a room, eating, giving and taking. The left is used for the opposite: leaving a bathroom, removing shoes.

It is a small thing that becomes automatic within about a week, and it is the easiest of these to start with.

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What counts as arrogance?
English: What counts as arrogance?

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What counts as arrogance?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said that nobody with an atom’s weight of kibr in his heart will enter Paradise. A man in the gathering heard that and asked the obvious question: what about a person who likes his clothes to look good, and his shoes? He was told that Allah is beautiful and loves beauty, and then given the definition. Kibr is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What counts as arrogance?
English: The reply matters as much as the warning. Somebody heard a hard statement, applied it to himself in the wrong place, and was corrected on the spot. Arrogance is not self-respect, tidiness or confidence.

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What does rejecting the truth mean in practice?
English: What does rejecting the truth mean in practice?

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What does rejecting the truth mean in practice?
English: Knowing you are wrong and not saying so. This is the half of the definition people skip, because from the inside it does not feel like arrogance. It feels like holding your ground. But refusing a correction because of who gave it, or because accepting it would be embarrassing, is exactly what is being named. It is far more common than looking down on anybody.

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What does this look like for me now?
English: It comes at you from two directions, and the second is the surprise. Someone will correct your prayer in a tone that has nothing to do with your prayer, and it will sting. But new certainty is its own risk. Three months in, it is easy to look at the family you came from, or at Muslims who seem casual about their religion, and quietly rank yourself above them. You have no idea what anybody else is carrying. And none of the people you are ranking know how long you will keep this up either.

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What is the opposite?
English: What is the opposite?

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What is the opposite?
English: Humility, and humility is not thinking badly of yourself. It is a step down that you choose to take, and the promise attached to it runs the other way. The Prophet ﷺ said that charity does not decrease wealth, that forgiving someone only increases their honour, and that no one humbles himself for Allah without Allah raising him. Each of the three names the thing you are afraid of losing and says you will not lose it.

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — Is wanting what someone has always wrong?
English: Is wanting what someone has always wrong?

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — Is wanting what someone has always wrong?
English: No, and the line between the two is clear. The Prophet ﷺ said not to wish to be like anyone except in two cases: a man Allah gave wealth, who spends it rightly, and a man Allah gave wisdom, who acts on it and teaches it. Wanting the same good for yourself, without wishing that they lose theirs, is allowed. Arabic has a separate word for it, ghibṭah. Ḥasad is wanting the thing taken away from them. Underneath, that is a complaint about who was given what, and it is aimed past the person at the One who gave it.

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — What actually stops it?
English: What actually stops it?

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — What actually stops it?
English: A change of direction, given as a practical instruction rather than as an attitude to adopt. When one of you looks at somebody who has been given more than him in wealth or in looks, the Prophet ﷺ said, let him look at someone who has less. Much of envy comes down to where the eye rests by habit. The instruction does not ask you to feel differently. It asks you to look somewhere else, and lets the feeling follow.

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — What does this look like for me now?
English: What converts envy is not usually money. It is someone reading Arabic without thinking about it, a family that eats together at iftar, twenty years of practice already behind them, a name that fits. Most of that cannot be wanted, because it is a childhood, and it has already happened. The permitted kind of wanting is for what is still open: you can want the Arabic and go and learn it, slowly, and badly at first. The rest is something to grieve rather than resent, and the two are not the same.

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — Where does envy sit?
English: Where does envy sit?

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — Where does envy sit?
English: The Prophet ﷺ named it in a list, and the company it keeps tells you how it is seen. Beware of suspicion, he said, for suspicion is the falsest of speech. Do not spy on one another, do not envy one another, do not turn away from one another, do not hate one another. Be servants of Allah, brothers. Every item on that list is a way one person’s private feelings quietly damage a group. Envy is counted among them, not treated as a harmless private feeling.

Where it appears: Was Islam spread by the sword? — And if someone still says no?
English: And if someone still says no?

Where it appears: Was Islam spread by the sword? — And if someone still says no?
English: Then it is their choice, and the Qur’an says so more than once. Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve. People who do not fight Muslims and have not driven them out are to be treated with kindness and justice, and the verse adds that God loves those who act justly. A Muslim who forces religion on anyone has left the religion’s own instructions, not followed them.

Where it appears: Was Islam spread by the sword? — Can anyone be forced to become Muslim?
English: Can anyone be forced to become Muslim?

Where it appears: Was Islam spread by the sword? — Can anyone be forced to become Muslim?
English: No, and the Qur’an says it in so many words: there is no compulsion in religion. It puts the same point to the Prophet ﷺ as a question. If God had willed, everyone on earth would have believed, so would you compel people to become believers? And it tells him what his job is and is not: you are only a reminder, you are not a controller over them. A belief held under threat is not the thing the Qur’an is asking for.

Where it appears: Was Islam spread by the sword? — How were people actually invited?
English: How were people actually invited?

Where it appears: Was Islam spread by the sword? — How were people actually invited?
English: By speaking. The Qur’an tells the Prophet ﷺ to invite with wisdom and good instruction, and to argue only in the best way. When he sent Muʿadh to Yemen, to a community of Jews and Christians, his instructions were to call them first to the testimony of faith, and only if they accepted it to teach them the prayer, and only then the zakat. To the two men he sent there together he said: make things easy for people, give them good news, and do not drive them away. That is the method the Prophet ﷺ taught, in his own words, to the people he put in charge.

Where it appears: Was Islam spread by the sword? — So what were the conquests?
English: So what were the conquests?

Where it appears: Was Islam spread by the sword? — So what were the conquests?
English: The spread of rule, which is not the spread of belief. Muslim states did expand by war, as every state of that age did, and the page on violence carries the limits the Qur’an set on fighting. What this question misses is that people under Muslim rule were not made Muslim. The verse that first permitted fighting says what it protects: monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques, named together. Egypt and Syria stayed largely Christian for centuries after Muslim rule began. And the country with the most Muslims in the world today, Indonesia, was reached by traders, not by an army.

Where it appears: Was Islam spread by the sword? — So what were the conquests?
English: If the person asking has a particular war in mind, you are allowed not to know it. "Empires fought wars, and Muslim ones did too. The religion forbids forcing belief, and here is where it says so" is an honest answer from someone new.

Where it appears: Was Islam spread by the sword? — What do I actually say?
English: "Nobody can be forced to believe. The Qur’an forbids it in so many words, and it names churches and synagogues as places to be protected. Empires spread by armies, and Muslim empires did too. The faith didn’t, and the biggest Muslim country in the world never saw one." Then stop. If they want the verses, they are above. If they want to argue about a century, that is a conversation about history, and you are allowed to say you are new and still learning.

Where it appears: What about Jesus? — Do Muslims believe in Jesus?
English: Do Muslims believe in Jesus?

Where it appears: What about Jesus? — Do Muslims believe in Jesus?
English: Yes, and it is not optional. A Muslim believes in every prophet God sent, and the Qur’an says believers make no distinction between them. It calls Jesus the Messiah and a word from God, tells of his birth to Mary when no man had touched her, and gives her a chapter of her own. Muslims say "peace be upon him" after his name, as they do after the name of every prophet.

Where it appears: What about Jesus? — How close are the two prophets?
English: How close are the two prophets?

Where it appears: What about Jesus? — How close are the two prophets?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said he is the nearest of all people to Jesus, that no prophet came between them, and that the prophets are brothers from one father. Their mothers differ, and their religion is one. Muslims see Muhammad ﷺ as the last in the same line Jesus belonged to, not as his rival.

Where it appears: What about Jesus? — So why not the Son of God?
English: So why not the Son of God?

Where it appears: What about Jesus? — So why not the Son of God?
English: Because the centre of Islam is that God is one, with nothing beside Him and nothing born of Him. The Qur’an says the Messiah was a messenger, that messengers had passed before him, and that he and his mother both ate food, which is its plain way of saying they were human. It compares his creation without a father to Adam’s creation without either. And it tells the People of the Scripture directly not to say "three". This is the real difference between the two faiths, and it is better named than talked around.

Where it appears: What about Jesus? — So why not the Son of God?
English: If the person asking is Christian, this is the point they will feel. You are not required to argue it. "This is where we differ" is a complete answer.

Where it appears: What about Jesus? — What about the crucifixion?
English: What about the crucifixion?

Where it appears: What about Jesus? — What about the crucifixion?
English: The Qur’an says he was not killed and not crucified, that it was made to appear so, and that God raised him to Himself. So Muslims do not believe he died for anyone’s sins. No soul carries another’s burden. Each person answers for their own deeds, and forgiveness comes from God directly, with nothing in between. If the next question is "then how are you saved?", the Prophet ﷺ answered it. Whoever testifies that there is no god but God, that Muhammad is His servant and messenger, and that Jesus is His servant and His word given to Mary, God will admit to Paradise, however few their good deeds.

Where it appears: What about Jesus? — What do I actually say?
English: "We believe in Jesus. We believe he was born of a virgin, and that he was the Messiah and a prophet of God. We don’t believe he was God or the Son of God, and that is the real difference between us." You can stop there. If it turns into a debate, the Qur’an gives you the line for that moment: for you is your religion, and for me is mine.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — Can I move at all?
English: Can I move at all?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — Can I move at all?
English: Scratching, shifting your weight, stepping forward to close a gap, picking up a child: none of this ends the prayer. What is meant by movement breaking it is a lot of it, continuously, for no reason connected to praying. The Prophet ﷺ prayed while carrying his granddaughter, putting her down to prostrate and picking her back up.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What about ordinary mistakes?
English: What about ordinary mistakes?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What about ordinary mistakes?
English: Losing count, forgetting a sitting, adding a movement, saying something in the wrong place: none of these break the prayer. They are fixed with two extra prostrations at the end, which the app covers separately. A beginner will do all of these, and none of them is a disaster.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What about ordinary mistakes?
English: The most common beginner mistake is starting the prayer over. Almost nothing requires that, and restarting turns a small slip into a long one.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: What actually breaks it?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: Losing your wudu. Speaking on purpose to someone. Eating or drinking. Laughing out loud. Turning your body right away from the qibla, or deciding to stop. If one of these happens, put it right and pray it again from the beginning. But read the rest of this page first, because almost every one of them has an exception, and most of what a beginner worries about is on the other list.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: Smiling is not laughing, and nobody has ever held that it breaks a prayer. What is meant is laughing aloud.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: Ibn al-Mundhir recorded the scholars as agreed that laughing aloud ends the prayer, and an-Nawawi and Ibn Qudamah both record that most of them held smiling does not. It is one of the few things on this page nobody argues about. One thing they do differ on is what else it costs you: the Maliki, Shafi`i and Hanbali schools hold that laughing aloud ends the prayer but leaves your wudu intact, so you stand up and pray again. The Hanafi school holds that it ends the wudu too, so someone following that school washes first. If you are not sure which applies to you, washing again costs a minute.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: What if I am facing the wrong way?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: This one is narrower than it sounds. What ends the prayer is turning your whole body away from the qibla with no reason to. Getting the direction wrong, in a hotel room or on a plane or in a city you do not know, does not, as long as you worked it out as best you could. If you find out afterwards that you were off, the prayer stands.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: A whole congregation once turned right around in the middle of Fajr, and their prayer counted.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: The people of Quba were praying facing Jerusalem when someone arrived to say the direction had been changed to the Ka`bah that night, so they turned mid-prayer and carried on. Bukhari puts the narration under a chapter heading that includes those who held there is no need to repeat a prayer offered by mistake in the wrong direction.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: What if I speak without thinking?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: A companion said "Allah have mercy on you" to a man who sneezed mid-prayer, not knowing he could not. Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ taught him, without scolding him and by his own account better than anyone had ever taught him anything, that this prayer is not the place for ordinary speech. He was not told to pray it again. Deliberate speech ends the prayer; speech before you knew the rule, or in a moment of forgetfulness, does not.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: This was not always the rule. People used to speak to each other in prayer and were told to stop, which is why the narrations about it read the way they do.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: Zayd ibn Arqam: "we used to speak while praying, and one of us would tell his companion what he needed, until the verse was revealed and we were ordered to be silent." Ibn Mas`ud used to greet the Prophet ﷺ mid-prayer and be answered, and returned from Abyssinia to find that he was not: "there is occupation enough in the prayer".

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I think I broke wudu?
English: What if I think I broke wudu?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I think I broke wudu?
English: Doubt does not. Someone asked the Prophet ﷺ about feeling as though they had passed wind mid-prayer, and he said not to leave the prayer unless they heard a sound or smelled something. Uncertainty is not enough. Carry on.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I think I broke wudu?
English: This is the hadith to remember if you find yourself checking constantly. The rule is deliberately strict about certainty, because doubt would otherwise end every prayer.

Where it appears: What happens after death — What happens in the grave?
English: What happens in the grave?

Where it appears: What happens after death — What happens in the grave?
English:
A question. The Prophet ﷺ described it plainly: when a person is laid in the grave and the people who buried them walk away, two angels come, sit them up, and ask what they said about this man, Muhammad. The believer answers that he is Allah’s servant and His Messenger, and is shown a place in the Fire and told that Allah has given a place in Paradise instead.

Read the answer again. It is the second half of the tashahhud, the words you say sitting in every prayer. You are already rehearsing it, five times a day, and the rehearsal is the preparation.

Where it appears: What happens after death — What happens in the grave?
English: People will tell you frightening things about the grave, some of them from narrations and some not. What is above is what the Prophet ﷺ said the believer meets. Hold on to that version.

Where it appears: What happens after death — What happens when I die?
English: What happens when I die?

Where it appears: What happens after death — What happens when I die?
English:
The same thing that happens to everyone. Every soul will taste death, the Qur’an says, and the full account is settled later, on the Day of Resurrection. Death is not the end of you. It is the end of the part where you can still choose, and the beginning of the part where what you chose is kept.

Islam’s whole shape points here. The prayer, the fast, the kindness to a parent: all of it is done by a person who knows this is coming and is getting ready. That is not morbid. It is the opposite of pretending.

Where it appears: What happens after death — What is the reckoning?
English: What is the reckoning?

Where it appears: What happens after death — What is the reckoning?
English:
Each person is handed their own record and told to read it. Nothing is missing from it: whoever did an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever did an atom’s weight of evil will see it. Then the scales are set, and the Qur’an promises that no soul will be wronged in the slightest.

That is the part people fear, and it is also the part that should steady you. The record is exact, so the quiet good you did that nobody noticed is in it. The judge is just, so nothing is held against you that you did not do. And the Prophet ﷺ said that nobody’s deeds alone will save them, not even his, unless Allah bestows His mercy. The scales are real. So is the hand on them.

Where it appears: What happens after death — What is the resurrection?
English: What is the resurrection?

Where it appears: What happens after death — What is the resurrection?
English: Everyone who ever lived, raised bodily, at once. The Qur’an answers the obvious objection in one line: someone asks who could give life to bones once they have crumbled, and the reply is that He who made them the first time will. The One who did it from nothing can do it again from dust. When the Day comes is known only to Allah, and working out dates for it is not part of believing in it.

Where it appears: What happens after death — What is the wait like?
English: What is the wait like?

Where it appears: What happens after death — What is the wait like?
English: The Qur’an calls it a barrier: behind the dead there is a barrier until the Day they are raised. How long that is, nobody knows, and it is not experienced as waiting in a room. What the narrations do say is that your account does not simply freeze. When a person dies their deeds end except three: a charity that keeps giving, knowledge that people still benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. So the things you set going in this life keep counting in the next.

Where it appears: What happens after death — Where does it end?
English: Where does it end?

Where it appears: What happens after death — Where does it end?
English:
In one of two places, and both are real. Of Paradise the Qur’an says that no soul knows what has been hidden for them, and the Prophet ﷺ said Allah has prepared for His servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined. The Fire is described too, and this page does not describe it, because you already know it is there.

What you may not know is what Allah wrote about Himself when He created everything: that His mercy overcomes His anger. A Muslim holds both facts at once and leans on the second. If the thought of the Day frightens you, let the fear move your feet towards the next prayer and then hand it back. Fear that freezes you is not the point of any of this.

Where it appears: What happens after death — Where does it end?
English: The page on repentance is the one to read next. It is short, and it is the reason none of this needs to be faced alone or without a way back.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Do I have to tell anyone what I did?
English: Do I have to tell anyone what I did?

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Do I have to tell anyone what I did?
English: There is no confession in Islam. No one at a mosque needs your history, no imam has to hear it, and nothing about becoming Muslim requires you to describe what you are leaving behind. Anyone who asks is asking for their own reasons, not for the religion, and you can decline.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Do I have to tell anyone what I did?
English: That includes online. You do not owe your story to a forum, a group chat, or anyone who says it will help others.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Does my past come with me?
English: Does my past come with me?

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Does my past come with me?
English:
A companion of the Prophet ﷺ, near the end of his own life, recalled that when Islam entered his heart he went to give his pledge, and was told that Islam demolishes what came before it. Not forgives it slowly. Demolishes it.

You did not arrive owing for those years. No debt carried over, no probation, nothing to work off.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Is it only cancelled?
English: Is it only cancelled?

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Is it only cancelled?
English: No, the Qur’an goes further than cancelling it. For those who turn back, believe and do right, it says their wrongs are exchanged for good. Not merely wiped out, but swapped. Read that twice, because it is not what most people expect a religion to say about their worst years.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — What about the things that have not gone away?
English: What about the things that have not gone away?

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — What about the things that have not gone away?
English:
Some of the past is not past. A marriage, children, a job, money, family who do not know. Those are real, and they do not vanish. There are no rulings on them here, because each has conditions on it and needs somebody who knows your situation.

What is already settled is the part underneath: none of it disqualifies you, and none of it has to be solved before you pray tonight.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — What about the things that have not gone away?
English: Take these one at a time and slowly. A convert given six life decisions in their first month usually makes them badly.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Why do I still feel guilty?
English: Why do I still feel guilty?

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Why do I still feel guilty?
English: Guilt often lingers, and it is not a sign that something was left undone. The Qur’an tells people who have wronged themselves not to despair, and it is addressed to them specifically, not to people with nothing to regret. Feeling guilty is not evidence against you.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Why do I still feel guilty?
English: If it becomes heavy rather than passing, that is worth telling a person you trust.

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — Does their reaction change what I owe them?
English: Does their reaction change what I owe them?

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — Does their reaction change what I owe them?
English:
No. The verse that tells you not to obey parents who press you to give up belief in God alone tells you, in the same sentence, to keep their company in this world with kindness. Both halves are the instruction, and the second does not wait for them to come round.

Asmāʾ, the daughter of Abū Bakr, was visited by her mother while her mother was still a pagan and wanted help from her. She asked the Prophet ﷺ whether she should keep good relations with her, and he told her yes. That is a parent who did not share her daughter’s religion, and the answer was to keep her close.

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — How long does this take?
English: How long does this take?

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — How long does this take?
English:
Longer than you would like, and it is not in your hands. The Qur’an tells the Prophet ﷺ himself that he does not guide whom he loves; Allah guides whom He wills. If he could not make the people he loved believe, you are not failing when you cannot either. Your job is to stay kind and stay in the room. Whether they ever come round is not your job, and it was never the condition for being good to them.

Families that shouted in the first month are often at the table in the third year. Keep the door open and let the years do the work.

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — What do I refuse, and what do I not?
English: What do I refuse, and what do I not?

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — What do I refuse, and what do I not?
English:
The refusal is narrow. It covers the thing being asked of you, not the relationship. Being asked to skip a prayer so there is no scene is the thing to decline. Being asked to come to dinner is not. Being asked to drink to prove you are still one of them is the thing to decline. Being asked to help your father in the garden is not.

The Qur’an says God does not forbid you from being good and fair to people who have not fought you over your religion. A parent who is upset with you has not fought you. Be good to them, and hold the line where it actually is.

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — What do I refuse, and what do I not?
English: Say the boundary once, kindly, in plain words: “I don’t drink now, but I would love to come.” Then stop explaining it. A boundary re-argued at every visit becomes the row you were trying to avoid.

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — What if it is not safe at home?
English: What if it is not safe at home?

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — What if it is not safe at home?
English: Then leave, and sort out the explanations later. Nothing in your religion asks you to stay somewhere you are in danger, and praying where nobody can see you is not a lesser prayer. If you cannot leave yet, find one person outside the house who knows the whole situation: a friend, someone at a mosque, or one of the helplines on the page about who to talk to. They are used to this, and they will not need you to explain your religion first.

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — Who can I lean on while it is hard?
English: Who can I lean on while it is hard?

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — Who can I lean on while it is hard?
English: One Muslim who knows your whole story, so that you are not carrying it alone. The imam at a nearby mosque, for the questions that depend on your particular family. And, for the nights when it is too much, a helpline. The page about who to talk to lists them. You do not have to be in crisis to call one.

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — Why are they reacting like this?
English: Why are they reacting like this?

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — Why are they reacting like this?
English:
Usually because they think they have lost you. A parent hears that you have changed religion and hears, underneath it, that you have rejected the home you were raised in, and that you will now be a stranger at their table. Some of it is fear of what they have seen on the news. Some of it is grief. Almost none of it is a considered view of Islam, which is why arguing the case rarely helps in the first months.

What changes their mind, when it changes, is watching you. A son who calls more than he used to, a daughter who is calmer than she was. Time and conduct do what no conversation can.

Where it appears: What if my family doesn’t accept my Islam? — Why are they reacting like this?
English: The questions they will actually ask, about violence, about Jesus, about why you cannot eat what they cook, each have a page of their own. Read those before the next visit, not during it.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it belief, or practice?
English: Is it belief, or practice?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it belief, or practice?
English: When the angel Jibril asked the Prophet ﷺ about this in front of his companions, the answer came in two parts: what you believe, and what you do. Neither stands alone. That is why this app teaches the prayer and the belief side by side rather than one first and one later.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it meant to be this hard?
English: Is it meant to be this hard?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it meant to be this hard?
English: You are not behind. The Prophet ﷺ said the religion is easy, and that whoever overburdens themselves in it will not keep it up, so take the next thing rather than all of it. The Qur’an says God does not ask of anyone more than they can bear.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does it ask of me?
English: What does it ask of me?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does it ask of me?
English: The testimony of faith, the five daily prayers, zakat, a yearly share of savings given to those entitled to it, fasting in Ramadan, and the pilgrimage to Mecca once in a lifetime for anyone able to make it. The Prophet ﷺ described Islam as built on these five.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does the word mean?
English: What does the word mean?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does the word mean?
English: Islam is an Arabic word meaning submission, giving yourself over to God. A Muslim is someone who does that. It comes from the same root as salam, peace, and the two ideas sit together: peace through no longer being pulled in every direction at once.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What is at the centre of it?
English: What is at the centre of it?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What is at the centre of it?
English: Everything else rests on this. Islam teaches that there is one God, Allah, the Arabic word for God used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews too, and that worship belongs to Him alone, with nothing and no one sharing it. Saying and meaning that is what makes a person Muslim.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What is at the centre of it?
English: Nobody can be forced into this. The Qur’an says plainly that there is no compulsion in religion.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Am I already reading it?
English: Am I already reading it?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Am I already reading it?
English: The Qur’an is not only read, it is recited, in every prayer, out loud or quietly. Al-Fatihah, its opening chapter of seven short verses, is said in every unit of every prayer for the rest of your life. Learning it is the single most useful thing a new Muslim can memorise.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Am I already reading it?
English: Until you know it, say what you can and keep learning. Nobody starts fluent, and the Practice screen exists to take it a line at a time.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — What do Muslims believe it is?
English: What do Muslims believe it is?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — What do Muslims believe it is?
English: Not a book about God, but the speech of God, revealed in Arabic to Muhammad ﷺ through the angel Jibril over about twenty-three years, and preserved unchanged since. That is the claim, and it is why the Arabic itself matters so much: a translation is understood as an explanation of the Qur’an rather than the Qur’an.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Where should I start?
English: Where should I start?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Where should I start?
English: Start small and start with sound. Learn Al-Fatihah, then a few of the short chapters at the end, listening and repeating rather than reading silently. The Prophet ﷺ said the best of people are those who learn the Qur’an and teach it. Learning it is the point, and it is slow for everyone.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Why does it not start at the beginning?
English: Why does it not start at the beginning?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Why does it not start at the beginning?
English: It has 114 chapters, called surahs, made of verses called ayahs. They are not in the order they were revealed, and it is not a story told front to back, so reading it cover to cover like a novel is not how most people start, and struggling with that is not a failure of yours.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Are all hadith reliable?
English: Are all hadith reliable?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Are all hadith reliable?
English: No. Because hadith were passed on by people, scholars spent centuries grading them, examining every chain and every narrator. Some are sound, some are weak, and some are forgeries. That is why this app names its sources: so you can check, rather than take its word.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Are all hadith reliable?
English: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim are the two collections Sunni scholars regard as the most rigorously authenticated. Other collections contain both strong and weak reports, which is why a grading matters there and not in these two.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does it look like day to day?
English: Much of it is small and human: not harming a neighbour, making a guest welcome, saying something good or staying quiet, eating with the right hand, a few words before sleeping. Following the Sunnah is not an extra layer of difficulty on top of the religion. A lot of it is simply how a decent person moves through a day.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does it look like day to day?; Sincerity — What does it look like day to day?
English: What does it look like day to day?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does Sunnah mean?
English: What does Sunnah mean?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does Sunnah mean?
English: Sunnah means a way or a path, and specifically the way the Prophet ﷺ lived: what he said, what he did, and what he approved of in others. It reaches us through hadith, which are reports of those things recorded with the chain of people who passed each one down.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Why does it sit beside the Qur’an?
English: Why does it sit beside the Qur’an?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Why does it sit beside the Qur’an?
English: The Qur’an gives the command and the Sunnah usually gives the method. "Establish the prayer" appears again and again; how many units, when, and what to say in them comes from watching him. The Qur’an itself instructs Muslims to take what the Messenger gives them.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I recite?
English: What do I recite?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I recite?
English:
Al-Fatihah, in every rakʿah of every prayer. Aloud in some prayers and quietly in others; the guide tells you which. It is the one text the prayer cannot do without, and it has a page and a screen of its own, verse by verse, with the recording against each verse.

In the first two rakʿahs a short surah follows it. Al-Ikhlas is where most people start. It is not required, and a prayer of Al-Fatihah alone is complete.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I recite?
English: Learn Al-Fatihah first and the rest of this page second. Until you know it, read it from the screen, and say what you know of it.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say bowing?
English: What do I say bowing?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say bowing?
English: Bent from the waist with your back straight and your hands on your knees. Once you have settled there, three times.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say in the sitting?
English: What do I say in the sitting?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say in the sitting?
English: Sitting, with your right index finger raised. After the second rakʿah in any prayer longer than two, and again at the very end. It greets Allah, the Prophet ﷺ, and every righteous servant, and closes with the testimony of faith. It is the longest text here, and the one that most repays learning slowly.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say once I am standing?
English: What do I say once I am standing?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say once I am standing?
English: Quietly, with your right hand resting over your left forearm on your chest, in the first rakʿah only. It is praise, said before anything is asked for.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say prostrating?
English: What do I say prostrating?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say prostrating?
English: With your forehead, nose, palms, knees and toes on the ground. Once settled, three times. You prostrate twice in every rakʿah, with a short sitting between.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say sitting between them?
English: What do I say sitting between them?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say sitting between them?
English: Sitting up between the two prostrations. Three words.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say standing back up?
English: What do I say standing back up?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What do I say standing back up?
English: As you rise from bowing, until you are standing upright and still. The first half says that Allah hears you; the second answers it with praise.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What ends the prayer?
English: What ends the prayer?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What ends the prayer?
English: Turn your head to the right and say it. Then to the left, and say it again. The prayer ends on the second one. You are greeting whoever is beside you, and the angels, so you turn even when you pray alone.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What follows it at the end?
English: What follows it at the end?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What follows it at the end?
English: In the final sitting only, straight after the tashahhud. Prayers on the Prophet ﷺ and his family, as they were sent on Ibrahim.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What is the line before the Qur’an?
English: What is the line before the Qur’an?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What is the line before the Qur’an?
English: Still quietly, once, before you recite. A single line asking Allah’s protection from Shayṭān.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What opens the prayer?
English: What opens the prayer?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — What opens the prayer?
English: Two words, said with your hands raised to shoulder level. From that moment you are in prayer. You say the same two words at every change of position afterwards: going down to bow, going down to prostrate, sitting up, and standing for the next rakʿah. It is the text you will say most.

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — Why is it all in Arabic?
English: Why is it all in Arabic?

Where it appears: What to say in prayer — Why is it all in Arabic?
English: Because every Muslim, in every country, says the same words. That is why you can walk into any mosque on earth and pray behind whoever is leading. The words are fewer than they look: ten short texts, and most of them are a single line. Read them from the screen until they stick, and know what you are saying while you learn to say it.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I covered, and is the place clean?
English: Am I covered, and is the place clean?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I covered, and is the place clean?
English: The Qur’an tells people to take their adornment at every place of prayer, so dress as you would to meet someone you respect. Your clothes and the ground you pray on should be clean. A carpet, a towel or a mat is fine; a prayer mat is convenient, not required.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I covered, and is the place clean?
English: How much has to be covered differs a little between men and women and is set out in the clothing guide. Ordinary loose clothes cover it for most people.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I in wudu?
English: Am I in wudu?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I in wudu?
English: Wudu is the short wash before prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said the prayer of someone who has broken it is not accepted until they wash again. One wudu covers several prayers. It lasts until something breaks it, and the wudu guide sets out what does and what only feels as though it does.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Do I have to say the intention?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: The intention is a thought, not a sentence: knowing which prayer you are about to pray. You do not say it out loud, and you do not need a formula. If you are standing on a mat about to pray Maghrib, you have already intended it.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Some people are taught to say the intention aloud. Scholars differ on whether that is recommended, and nobody holds that the prayer fails without it.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English:
Most of this is agreed, and only one part is open. The imams agree that the intention lives in the heart and that the prayer never asks you to speak it, so that is not one side of an argument. What they differ on is whether saying it aloud is recommended.

Ibn Taymiyyah records both views. Scholars among the followers of Abu Hanifah, ash-Shafi`i and Ahmad held it recommended, as a way of making the intention firmer. Scholars among the followers of Malik and Ahmad held that it is not, because neither the Prophet ﷺ nor his Companions did it. He takes the second view. If you were taught to say it, saying it harms nothing.
