Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Scholars of the school held that voicing the intention is recommended, as a way of making it firmer. The same view is found among Shafi`i and Hanbali scholars.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Scholars of the school held that voicing it is not recommended, since neither the Prophet ﷺ nor his Companions did it. The same view is found among Hanbali scholars.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: Is it the right time?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: Each prayer has a window, and you pray inside it rather than whenever you like. The Qur’an calls prayer a decree of specified times. The Today screen works the times out from where you are, on the phone itself, so you do not have to calculate anything.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: If your local mosque prints a timetable and it differs from the app by a few minutes, follow the mosque.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English:
The app works the times out from the position of the sun, which is arithmetic. A mosque timetable involves decisions: which twilight angle to use for Fajr and ʿIsha, whether to round to the nearest five minutes, whether to hold ʿIsha back in summer so people can get there. Both are honest answers to the same question, and they land a few minutes apart.

Praying with the congregation you actually pray with matters more than the arithmetic. The differences are almost always small enough that either time falls inside the window. The one place worth checking is high summer in a northern country, where Fajr and ʿIsha can crowd together and mosques handle it in noticeably different ways.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Which way do I face?
English: Which way do I face?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Which way do I face?
English: Muslims face the Kaʿbah in Mecca, and the Qur’an gives that instruction directly. The Qibla screen in this app points the way from where you are. If you cannot work it out, on a plane or in an unfamiliar place, face your best guess and pray; that is accepted.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — Am I qualified to say anything?
English: Am I qualified to say anything?

Where it appears: When someone asks you — Am I qualified to say anything?
English: To pass on what you actually know, yes. The Prophet ﷺ said to convey from him even a single verse. That is a deliberately low bar, and it is about accuracy rather than credentials. What you are not qualified to do is answer questions you have not been taught the answer to. The difference between those two things is what this page is about.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What do I say when I do not know?
English: What do I say when I do not know?

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What do I say when I do not know?
English:
"I don’t know." Then, if you can, "let’s find out." That is a complete answer, it is honest, and scholars say it constantly. The ones worth listening to say it more often than anyone.

The temptation is to fill the gap, because being asked feels like being trusted, and saying nothing feels like letting somebody down. It is not. Guessing at a ruling for somebody who will act on it is far worse than a pause.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What do I say when I do not know?
English: Watch for the question that is really about somebody’s own situation: a marriage, money, family. Those need a person who can ask questions back, and that is rarely you.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What if I know the answer differs?
English: What if I know the answer differs?

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What if I know the answer differs?
English:
Say so. "There is more than one view on that, and mine is what my mosque follows" is more useful to a beginner than one confident answer, because it prepares them for the day somebody tells them otherwise.

Being given one confident answer is the thing most likely to have been done to you, and the easiest thing not to pass on.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What is actually worth passing on?
English: What is actually worth passing on?

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What is actually worth passing on?
English:
The things nobody told you. What happens in the first ten minutes at a mosque. That a short prayer counts. That your name stays. That the guilt about the years before is not evidence of anything.

Those are not advanced knowledge and they do not need a scholar. They are the things that were invisible to everybody who could have told you, and you are the only person likely to think of them.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — Why would anyone ask me?
English: Why would anyone ask me?

Where it appears: When someone asks you — Why would anyone ask me?
English: Because you remember not knowing, and almost nobody else in the room does. Somebody raised Muslim cannot tell you what is confusing about wudu, because it was never confusing to them. You can. That is a real thing to have, and it arrives at about year two whether you feel ready or not.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Is this Islam or is it their culture?
English: Is this Islam or is it their culture?

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Is this Islam or is it their culture?
English:
Sometimes it is culture, and it is fair to ask which. A useful question, asked plainly and without edge: **is that required, or is that how it is done where you are from?** Most people answer it honestly, and the ones who cannot were never going to be a good source.

The five categories of ruling are worth having in your head for exactly this. Much of what reaches you as a rule is a recommendation, and some of it is a habit.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Is this Islam or is it their culture?
English: Being told that this app, or a book, is wrong is also normal. Ask what it should say instead, and where that comes from. That is not rude. It is the ordinary way these things are discussed.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — What if they were unkind about it?
English: What if they were unkind about it?

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — What if they were unkind about it?
English:
Then they were wrong about the manner, whatever they were right about in substance. Being correct does not give anyone licence to be harsh, and a religion whose Prophet ﷺ was known for gentleness does not hand anybody the right to humiliate a stranger at prayer.

You are allowed to be hurt by it. What matters is not to conclude that the room, or the religion, is what that one person was.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — What if they were unkind about it?
English: If a particular mosque is consistently like this, try another one. They differ enormously, and moving is not a failure of patience.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — What should I actually say?
English: What should I actually say?

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — What should I actually say?
English:
"Thank you, I will look into it." That is a complete answer. It is true, and it ends the exchange without agreeing or arguing. You do not owe anyone a defence of what you were doing. You do not have to explain that you are new, and you certainly do not have to debate it in a prayer hall.

Then look into it, once, when you are calm. If two answers are still standing, follow the one your mosque follows.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Why did someone correct me in front of everyone?
English: Why did someone correct me in front of everyone?

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Why did someone correct me in front of everyone?
English:
It happens to almost everyone, and it is better to be ready for it than winded by it. Somebody will tell you your feet are wrong, your hands are in the wrong place, or that what you just did is not how it is done. It will usually be in the middle of a room, usually meant well, and usually said with no idea that you have been Muslim for six weeks.

It is not a judgement on whether you belong there. It is a mosque doing what mosques do, and it happens to people who have prayed for forty years.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Why do two people tell me opposite things?
English: Why do two people tell me opposite things?

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Why do two people tell me opposite things?
English:
Almost always because they follow different schools of thought, and each is describing their own correctly. Where to put your hands, whether to say the intention aloud, how many times to wipe: these are points where the scholarship genuinely differs, and has for a thousand years.

Neither of them is lying to you, and neither is making it up. You have walked into an old disagreement that nobody explained to you first.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Why do two people tell me opposite things?
English: That the schools differ on details of practice within Sunni Islam is not itself controversial. This app teaches one clear way, because a first-timer needs a path, and it marks the places where you will actually meet a difference.

Where it appears: When someone dies — How do I pray the funeral prayer?
English: How do I pray the funeral prayer?

Where it appears: When someone dies — How do I pray the funeral prayer?
English:
You stand in a row and follow the imam, and you stay standing the whole way through. There is no bowing and no prostration, which surprises almost everyone the first time. The imam says **Allāhu akbar** four times, and between them there are quiet supplications. Then the salam, and it is finished.

If you do not know the words, stand with everyone and say nothing. Following in silence still counts as taking part.

Where it appears: When someone dies — How do I pray the funeral prayer?
English: Four takbirs, standing, with no bowing and no prostration: the schools agree on that. What is said quietly between the takbirs is where they differ in detail.

Where it appears: When someone dies — How do I pray the funeral prayer?
English: You do not need wudu to attend, but you do need it to pray, the same as for any prayer.

Where it appears: When someone dies — Should I go if I did not know them?
English: Should I go if I did not know them?

Where it appears: When someone dies — Should I go if I did not know them?
English: Yes. Attending a funeral is encouraged even for a stranger. The Prophet ﷺ described a reward for whoever attends until the prayer, and a greater one for whoever stays until the burial. Turning up to a janazah for somebody you never met is an ordinary thing to do.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What actually happens at a janazah?
English: What actually happens at a janazah?

Where it appears: When someone dies — What actually happens at a janazah?
English: It happens quickly, and with very little ceremony. The body is washed and wrapped. A short prayer is prayed over it, usually at a mosque and often straight after one of the daily prayers. Then it is buried, normally within a day. There is no open casket, no music, and no long service.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What actually happens at a janazah?
English: It moves fast. If you hear in the morning, the burial may be that afternoon. That is normal, and not a sign that anybody is rushing.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What do I say to the family?
English: What do I say to the family?

Where it appears: When someone dies — What do I say to the family?
English:
Very little, and that is right. "May Allah have mercy on them" is enough, and so is saying nothing at all. Sit with people, make tea, take the children out. Grief in Islam is not silenced. Crying is not a failing, and no one has to pretend to be composed.

What is avoided is loud, staged mourning, and any suggestion that the family should be over it.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What do I say to the family?
English: Do not tell somebody their loss was a test they passed, or that it was for the best. Neither is comfort, and both are said constantly.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What do I say when I hear?
English: What do I say when I hear?

Where it appears: When someone dies — What do I say when I hear?
English:
The words people say when they hear that someone has died come from the Qur’an: **Innā li-llāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn**, to Allah we belong, and to Him we return. Say it quietly, to yourself. No one is waiting to hear it.

You say it for anyone. It is not only for Muslims, and it is not only for people you were close to.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What if the person who died was not Muslim?
English: What if the person who died was not Muslim?

Where it appears: When someone dies — What if the person who died was not Muslim?
English: Then the funeral will not look like this, and you are still allowed to grieve them, attend, and be with your family. What you may and may not take part in depends on what the funeral involves. That is a question for somebody who knows both your family and the situation, not for an app.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What if the person who died was not Muslim?
English: Ask someone before the day rather than on it. Imams are asked this often, and it will not surprise them.

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — Does this ever affect the five prayers?
English: Does this ever affect the five prayers?

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — Does this ever affect the five prayers?
English: No. A prayer that is due is prayed in its window, and a prayer you slept through or forgot is prayed as soon as you remember it, whatever the sun is doing. The Prophet ﷺ said there is no making up for a forgotten prayer except to pray it when you remember.

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — Does this ever affect the five prayers?
English: Schools differ on whether a missed prayer may be made up at the three sun-bound times themselves, and on which voluntary prayers with a reason may go ahead.

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — Does this ever affect the five prayers?
English: This app teaches the wider view, because it is the one the Missing a prayer page already follows: pray a missed prayer when you remember it. If your mosque follows the Hanafi school, it will hold the three sun-bound moments back even for a missed prayer, and following your mosque is right.

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — Does this ever affect the five prayers?
English: At the three sun-bound times no prayer is offered, not even a missed one; the day’s own ʿAsr is the exception as the sun sets. After Fajr and after ʿAsr, voluntary prayer is forbidden but a missed prayer may be made up.

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — Does this ever affect the five prayers?
English: Any prayer with a reason goes ahead at all of these times: a missed prayer, the funeral prayer, the two rakʿahs after tawaf, greeting the mosque. Only voluntary prayer with no particular reason is forbidden. Hanbali scholars hold the same in one of two views, and it is the view of Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn Bāz and Ibn ʿUthaymīn.

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — When is voluntary prayer forbidden?
English: When is voluntary prayer forbidden?

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — When is voluntary prayer forbidden?
English: Three times a day, all tied to the sun. The Prophet ﷺ named them together, and the prayer-times page in this app marks them on the day.

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — When is voluntary prayer forbidden?
English: These are about voluntary prayers, the ones you choose to add. Nothing here stops you praying one of the five.

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — Why is there no sunnah after Fajr and ʿAsr?
English: Why is there no sunnah after Fajr and ʿAsr?

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — Why is there no sunnah after Fajr and ʿAsr?
English: Because of two more spans, tied to your own prayer rather than to the sun. Once you have prayed Fajr, voluntary prayer is forbidden until the sun is up; once you have prayed ʿAsr, until it has set. That is why the Every prayer page shows no sunnah after those two, and why the early morning and the late afternoon are the quiet stretches of the day.

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — Why these times?
English: Why these times?

Where it appears: When voluntary prayer is forbidden — Why these times?
English: The Prophet ﷺ told his companions not to time their prayer to the sun’s rising or setting, but to wait until it was fully up or fully gone, because the sun rises and sets between the two horns of a devil: the moments when those who worship the sun bow to it. A Muslim’s prayer must not look like theirs, even by accident of the clock.

Where it appears: When you are angry — Is it weak to hold back?
English: Is it weak to hold back?

Where it appears: When you are angry — Is it weak to hold back?
English: The opposite. The strong person, the Prophet ﷺ said, is not the one who wins a wrestling match. The strong one is the one who keeps hold of himself at the moment of anger. Nothing in this asks you to be timid or to let yourself be walked over. It moves the idea of strength from winning the exchange to the self-control it takes not to have it.

Where it appears: When you are angry — So am I sinning for feeling angry?
English: So am I sinning for feeling angry?

Where it appears: When you are angry — So am I sinning for feeling angry?
English: No. Anger arrives without being chosen, and there is anger in the Prophet’s ﷺ own life over things that deserved it. What is asked of you is a gap between feeling it and acting on it: leaving the room, saying nothing for a minute, saying the words above. The instruction is about what you do next, not about what you feel.

Where it appears: When you are angry — What do I actually do in the moment?
English: What do I actually do in the moment?

Where it appears: When you are angry — What do I actually do in the moment?
English: Two men were arguing in front of the Prophet ﷺ until one of them was red in the face. The Prophet ﷺ said he knew a sentence which, if the man said it, would take away what he was feeling: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shayṭān. It is short enough to say through clenched teeth, and that is the point. It is not something to reflect on later. It is something to reach for while the anger is happening.

Where it appears: When you are angry — What do I actually do in the moment?
English: The narration ends with the man refusing to say it: "I am not mad." Anger always argues that it is reasonable, and it is the one state in which advice feels like an insult. Knowing that in advance is most of the help.

Where it appears: When you are angry — What does this look like for me now?
English: A relative will say something about your religion that is wrong, and said to wound. It will happen when you are tired, in front of other people, and about the thing you care most about. How you answer is the only thing about Islam most of them will ever look at closely. That is unfair, and it is true. You are allowed to end a conversation. You are not required to win it.

Where it appears: When you are angry — What does this look like for me now?; Thinking you are better — What does this look like for me now?; Wanting what someone else has — What does this look like for me now?; Doing it to be seen — What does this look like for me now?; Patience and gratitude — What does this look like for me now?
English: What does this look like for me now?

Where it appears: When you are angry — Why is this the advice he kept repeating?
English: Why is this the advice he kept repeating?

Where it appears: When you are angry — Why is this the advice he kept repeating?
English: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ asking for advice and was told: do not become angry. He asked again, and got the same answer. He asked a third time, and heard the same again. It is one of the shortest instructions in the hadith collections, and it was given to somebody who wanted a whole programme, because anger is the point at which most people lose everything else they have learned.

Where it appears: When you don’t know everything yet — Can I pray before I know all of it?
English: Can I pray before I know all of it?

Where it appears: When you don’t know everything yet — Can I pray before I know all of it?
English:
Yes. The guides in this app walk you through a prayer at its fullest: every position, every word, in order. That is what to aim at, but it is not the bar. A prayer done briefly and plainly, with the essentials in place, is a prayer. It is not half a prayer, and it does not need making up later.

Reading "23 steps" on a night when you have four minutes and no confidence can make praying feel out of reach. It is not.

Where it appears: When you don’t know everything yet — Can I pray before I know all of it?
English: On a hard day, the least is the right amount.

Where it appears: When you don’t know everything yet — Is it better to rush it or pray it late?
English: Is it better to rush it or pray it late?

Where it appears: When you don’t know everything yet — Is it better to rush it or pray it late?
English: The prayer has fixed times, and the time is part of it. Given the choice between a short prayer inside its window and a careful one after the window has closed, pray the short one. The full shape will come later. The time will not come back.

Where it appears: When you don’t know everything yet — What actually has to be there?
English: What actually has to be there?

Where it appears: When you don’t know everything yet — What actually has to be there?
English: A man once prayed in the mosque and the Prophet ﷺ told him three times to go back and pray, because he had not prayed. The man asked to be taught, and what he was taught is the shortest description of a prayer there is.

Where it appears: When you don’t know everything yet — What actually has to be there?
English: The word doing the work is "settle". Rushing is the one thing that narration corrects, and it corrects it three times.

Where it appears: When you don’t know everything yet — What if I only know Al-Fatihah?
English: What if I only know Al-Fatihah?

Where it appears: When you don’t know everything yet — What if I only know Al-Fatihah?
English: Then you have what you need. Al-Fatihah is the part the prayer cannot do without, and anything after it is extra rather than necessary. If you are still learning the words, read them from the screen. No one has to know them by heart before they are allowed to start.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — How is it received?
English: How is it received?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — How is it received?
English: The Prophet ﷺ described God as more pleased with a person’s repentance than someone would be who lost their camel in the desert and then found it. The image is not of a grudging pardon. It is relief and delight.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — Is it too late for me?
English: Is it too late for me?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — Is it too late for me?
English: The Qur’an addresses people who have wronged themselves and tells them not to despair of God’s mercy, because He forgives all sins. That verse is worth knowing early, because the thing most likely to end someone’s practice is not a sin. It is deciding afterwards that they are past helping.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What does repentance actually take?
English: What does repentance actually take?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What does repentance actually take?
English: Stopping, meaning it, and asking. There is no ritual, no witness, and nobody to confess to. You turn to God directly. The Qur’an calls it turning to Him with sincere repentance, and that is all it takes.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What if I do it again?
English: What if I do it again?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What if I do it again?
English: You repent again. People expect to fail once and be finished. That is not how it works, and a habit that takes a year to break took a year for everybody else too. Keep praying while you work on it. Stopping the prayer because you feel unworthy of it is the one thing that makes it worse.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What if I do it again?
English: No one is owed an account of your sins. You do not have to tell an imam, a friend, or anyone at the mosque.

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — How does a Muslim know what Islam says?
English: How does a Muslim know what Islam says?

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — How does a Muslim know what Islam says?
English: By asking, in order, what the Qur’an says, what the Prophet ﷺ said and did, and what the scholars who spent their lives on both concluded from them. That order is not a custom. The Qur’an tells believers to obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and to take any dispute back to those two. Everything a Muslim calls a ruling has travelled that route, and knowing the route means you can ask where an answer came from instead of taking it on trust.

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — So what is fiqh?
English: So what is fiqh?

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — So what is fiqh?
English: The result. Fiqh is the body of rulings that reading produced: what is required, what is recommended, what is simply allowed, what is disliked, what is forbidden. Those five kinds are the next lesson, and they are the vocabulary every ruling is stated in. The four schools you will hear named are four traditions of doing this work, and all four are Sunni.

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — What does the Qur’an settle?
English: What does the Qur’an settle?

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — What does the Qur’an settle?
English: The commands and the limits. Pray, fast, give, be good to your parents, do not drink, do not take interest. It is short on method: it says to establish the prayer far more often than it says how, and it names what is forbidden in a few lines rather than a code. That is by design. The Qur’an gives the shape, and the next source fills it in.

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — What does the Sunnah add?
English: What does the Sunnah add?

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — What does the Sunnah add?
English: The method, and the detail. How many rakʿahs, what to say in them, what breaks a fast. The Prophet ﷺ lived the Qur’an in front of people who remembered and wrote down what he said and did, and those reports are the Sunnah. The Qur’an itself tells Muslims to take what the Messenger gives them. The page on the Sunnah explains how a report is graded and why not every one is reliable; here the point is only where it sits, second, and inseparable from the first.

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — Where do scholars come in?
English: Where do scholars come in?

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — Where do scholars come in?
English:
Most questions are not answered word for word in either source. Is a mortgage interest? Does a nicotine patch break a fast? What does a convert do about a wedding with no Muslim guardian? Somebody has to read the texts, weigh them, and reason from what they say to the case in front of them. That work is called ijtihād, and the people qualified to do it are scholars.

The Prophet ﷺ said that a judge who strives for the right answer is rewarded even when he gets it wrong, and twice when he gets it right. Reasoning carefully from the sources is not a departure from them. It is what the sources expect.

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — Where do scholars come in?
English: This is also why two scholars can give two answers to the same question. That has a page of its own, further along the path.

Where it appears: Where do Islamic rulings come from? — Who do I actually ask?
English: A person, for anything about your own life, because a page cannot hear the part that changes the answer. An imam at a mosque near you is the usual first person. When you get an answer, it is fair to ask where it comes from: a verse, a narration, a school’s position. A good answer can say. And an answer that arrived by this route is worth more than a confident one that did not.

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — Do I have to choose?
English: Do I have to choose?

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — Do I have to choose?
English: No. The Qur’an being best does not mean dropping everything else for it, and the scholars say so directly. Read the Qur’an when the time is yours, and every letter is rewarded ten times over. Say the dhikr of the moment when its moment comes. Keep the four phrases for the gaps in the day. Someone who does all three has not chosen between them. They have a day with a shape.

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — Do I have to choose?
English: Ten spare minutes, then: first the adhkar of whatever moment you are in, if there is one. Then the Qur’an, from wherever you left off. The four phrases go with you through the rest of the day.

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — What if I only have a minute?
English: What if I only have a minute?

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — What if I only have a minute?
English: Say the words Allah loves most. Asked which words were best, the Prophet ﷺ answered: the ones Allah chose for His angels and His servants, subḥāna-llāhi wa bi-ḥamdih. He also named four phrases as the dearest to Allah, subḥāna-llāh, al-ḥamdu li-llāh, lā ilāha illa-llāh and Allāhu akbar, and said it does not matter which you begin with. A minute is enough for all four.

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — What if I only have a minute?
English: The dua book has an occasion on the merit of these four phrases, in the book’s own wording. It is one of the doors below.

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — When does something else come first?
English: When does something else come first?

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — When does something else come first?
English: When a dhikr belongs to that moment. Some remembrances have a time or a place of their own, and in that time they come before the Qur’an. The reason is simple: the Qur’an can be read at any hour, and a timed dhikr cannot. Miss its moment and it is gone. The Prophet ﷺ sought forgiveness three times the instant he finished a prayer, and told people to send more prayers on him on a Friday than on other days. Those are the moments. The app already holds most of them.

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — When does something else come first?
English: This is why the adhkar in this app sit at fixed times: the times are theirs. The Qur’an tab has no clock on it, because the Qur’an has none.

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — Which dhikr is best?
English:
The Qur’an, read with attention to what it says. The Qur’an calls itself the best of speech, and it calls itself the Reminder. The scholars draw the plain conclusion from that: an-Nawawi wrote that reciting the Qur’an is the finest dhikr, and Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn Baz and Ibn ʿUthaymin say the same. It is Allah’s own speech.

There is one exception, and the exception covers a lot of an ordinary day.

Where it appears: Which dhikr is best? — Which dhikr is best?
English: That reciting the Qur’an is the best dhikr in general is agreed. The same scholars who say so also say that a dhikr with a time of its own comes first when that time arrives.

Where it appears: Who can I talk to? — What can this app do, and what can it not?
English: What can this app do, and what can it not?

Where it appears: Who can I talk to? — What can this app do, and what can it not?
English: It can teach you what it already holds, with the radio off. It cannot answer back. When the search finds nothing, you can tell us what you were looking for, and a person reads those later to decide what to write next. Nobody reads them as they arrive and nobody replies, so it is not a way to reach anyone. For that, the people above are real.

Where it appears: Who can I talk to? — What if tonight is the hard part?
English: What if tonight is the hard part?

Where it appears: Who can I talk to? — What if tonight is the hard part?
English: New Muslims often carry the worst nights alone, because the people who would normally notice are the people they have not told. If you are frightened for yourself, or you do not want to be here any more, that is what these lines are for. There is nothing un-Islamic about calling one. The people on the other end will not judge you and will not need you to explain your religion.

Where it appears: Who can I talk to? — Who answers a question this app does not?
English: Who answers a question this app does not?

Where it appears: Who can I talk to? — Who answers a question this app does not?
English:
A person who knows you, or can hear the whole of your situation. For most people that is the imam at a mosque near them. Go for any prayer that is not Friday midday, wait until it ends, and say that you are new and have a question. That sentence is enough; it is one they hear often and are glad to.

Questions about your own life, a marriage, money, a job, a family that does not know yet, need a person for exactly this reason. A page cannot hear the part that changes the answer, which is why some pages in this app end with "ask someone qualified" rather than pretending to.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — How do I get to know Him?
English: How do I get to know Him?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — How do I get to know Him?
English: Through His names, rather than in the abstract, and you will meet them constantly.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — How do I get to know Him?
English: Learning a few is a gentler way in than trying to think about God in the abstract.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — Is Allah a different God?
English: Is Allah a different God?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — Is Allah a different God?
English: No. Allah is simply the Arabic word for God, and Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews use it when they pray.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — Is Allah a different God?
English: It has no plural and no gender, which is part of why Muslims keep the word rather than translating it.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What if I try to picture Him?
English: What if I try to picture Him?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What if I try to picture Him?
English: Any picture you form is wrong by definition, and you are not expected to form one.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What if I try to picture Him?
English: This is why Muslims do not depict God, and why you will not find images of Him anywhere in Islam.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What was said when the Prophet ﷺ was asked to describe God?
English: What was said when the Prophet ﷺ was asked to describe God?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What was said when the Prophet ﷺ was asked to describe God?
English: A short chapter of the Qur’an, and Muslims have taken it as the definition ever since.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Do Muslims worship him?
English: Do Muslims worship him?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Do Muslims worship him?
English: Muhammad ﷺ was born in Mecca around 570 CE and received the Qur’an over roughly twenty-three years. Muslims believe he is the last of a long line of prophets that includes Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa, or Abraham, Moses and Jesus. He is not divine and is not worshipped. He delivered the message; the message is from God.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What is the ﷺ after his name?
English: What is the ﷺ after his name?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What is the ﷺ after his name?
English: You will see ﷺ written after his name throughout this app and everywhere else. It stands for an Arabic phrase asking God to bless him and grant him peace. Muslims say it aloud out of respect whenever he is mentioned. Nobody will mind if you forget at first.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What was he like?
English: What was he like?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What was he like?
English: The Qur’an describes him as being of great character, and the people who lived with him described someone who never used foul or crude language and who taught that the best people are those with the best manners. Much of what Muslims try to imitate is not ritual at all. It is how he treated people.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Why follow him?
English: Why follow him?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Why follow him?
English: Because the Qur’an tells them to. It calls him an excellent example, and says that obeying him is obeying God. In practice this is very concrete: the Qur’an commands prayer without describing how, and the answer to "how" is that he said, "Pray as you have seen me praying."

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Why follow him?
English: Loving and following him is not the same as worshipping him. The distinction matters to Muslims and is worth being clear about early.

Where it appears: Whoever works for you — And if I do not pay?
English: And if I do not pay?

Where it appears: Whoever works for you — And if I do not pay?
English: The Prophet ﷺ named three people God will stand against on the Day of Resurrection. One who gives a promise in God’s name and breaks it, one who sells a free man and consumes the price, and one who hires a worker, takes the work in full, and does not give him his wage. Withholding pay is not filed with ordinary debts here. It is put beside breaking an oath sworn in God’s name.

Where it appears: Whoever works for you — What did he ﷺ call them?
English: What did he ﷺ call them?

Where it appears: Whoever works for you — What did he ﷺ call them?
English: Abu Dharr was seen wearing a cloak, with the man who served him wearing the same one. He explained why. He had insulted a man by his mother, and the Prophet ﷺ told him he still had something of the old ignorance in him, that these are your brothers whom God has placed under your hand, and that whoever has a brother under his hand should feed him from what he eats and clothe him from what he wears. Then the limit on the work itself. Do not ask of them more than they can do, and if you do, help them with it.

Where it appears: Whoever works for you — What did he ﷺ call them?
English: The narration is about a man who owned another. What carries across is the instruction about the gap in power, which is what it addresses.

Where it appears: Whoever works for you — When do they get paid?
English: When do they get paid?

Where it appears: Whoever works for you — When do they get paid?
English: Give the worker his wages before his sweat dries. That is the whole narration, and the timing in it is deliberate rather than poetic. Payment is due when the work is done, not when it suits the person who owes it. Most of what makes a late payment comfortable for the payer is that the cost of waiting lands entirely on somebody else.

Where it appears: Why can’t you eat that? — Is it just wine, or all of it?
English: Is it just wine, or all of it?

Where it appears: Why can’t you eat that? — Is it just wine, or all of it?
English: All of it. The Prophet ﷺ said that every intoxicant is khamr, the Qur’an’s word for wine, and every intoxicant is forbidden. Asked about the drinks brewed in Yemen from honey and from barley, he gave the same answer, so it is not about grapes. Beer, spirits and wine are one category, and the category is what is forbidden.

Where it appears: Why can’t you eat that? — Isn’t that a lot of rules about food?
English: Isn’t that a lot of rules about food?

Where it appears: Why can’t you eat that? — Isn’t that a lot of rules about food?
English: It is fewer than it looks. The Qur’an tells believers not to forbid the good things God has made lawful, and asks who has forbidden the good provision He produced for His servants. It also says plainly that the food of the People of the Scripture is lawful for Muslims, so a Muslim can eat at a Christian or Jewish table. The page on food carries the one live question about meat, which is not whether such meat is lawful in principle but how modern slaughter measures up.

Where it appears: Why can’t you eat that? — What about my family’s table?
English: What about my family’s table?

Where it appears: Why can’t you eat that? — What about my family’s table?
English: Keep sitting at it. Eat what you can, leave what you cannot without a speech, and answer questions when they come. If you are the guest, a quiet word to the host beforehand is kinder than a plate pushed away. Most families adjust faster when the change is undramatic, and the meal itself is the answer to the question underneath: that you are still theirs.

Where it appears: Why can’t you eat that? — What about my family’s table?
English: You do not owe anyone the reason. "I don’t eat pork" is complete. The reason is for when they are curious, not for when they are testing.

Where it appears: Why can’t you eat that? — What do I actually say?
English: "God set a few things aside: pork, alcohol, a couple of others. Everything else on this table is fine, and I’m glad to be at it." Then eat. If they want the verses, they are above. If they want to argue about health, that is a conversation about health, and it is not why you stopped.

Where it appears: Why can’t you eat that? — What is off the menu, and why?
English: What is off the menu, and why?

Where it appears: Why can’t you eat that? — What is off the menu, and why?
English: Four things, and the Qur’an names them: animals found dead, blood, the flesh of swine, and meat dedicated to anything other than God. Alcohol has its own verse, which calls intoxicants the work of Satan and says to avoid them. The reason the Qur’an gives is not health and not hygiene, though people will offer you both. It is that God has said so, and the verse begins with the word "only": the list is short, and everything else is lawful and good. The same verse adds that someone forced by hunger, not wanting it and not going past need, carries no sin.

Where it appears: Why do women cover? — Did the first Muslim women do this?
English: Did the first Muslim women do this?

Where it appears: Why do women cover? — Did the first Muslim women do this?
English: Yes, and at once. ʿAʾishah, the Prophet’s ﷺ wife, said of the women who had emigrated to Medina that when the verse about the head-covering came down they cut their waist-cloths at the edge and covered themselves with the pieces. It was the women’s own response to a verse, done the day they heard it. Nobody in the story is made to do anything.

Where it appears: Why do women cover? — Is it about hiding women away?
English: Is it about hiding women away?

Where it appears: Why do women cover? — Is it about hiding women away?
English: The verse says the opposite: that a woman be recognised, and left alone. The Qur’an calls clothing itself a gift from God, given to cover and to adorn, and then says the clothing of righteousness is better still. Covering is one form of the modesty asked of everyone, in look and in manner before it is ever in cloth. The first Muslim women went out, prayed in the mosque, traded and taught, covered.

Where it appears: Why do women cover? — Is it about hiding women away?
English: The question is often really "were you made to?" Answer that one. "No. I chose this, and I would tell you if I hadn’t" does more than any verse.

Where it appears: Why do women cover? — What do I actually say?
English: "The Qur’an tells men to lower their eyes before it says anything about women’s clothes. Then it asks women to dress modestly, and it gives the reason: so they’re known for who they are and left alone. It’s an act of worship, it’s between her and God, and it was her choice." You can stop there. If the person is worried for you, or for her, answer the worry, not the argument.

Where it appears: Why do women cover? — What does the Qur’an actually say?
English: What does the Qur’an actually say?

Where it appears: Why do women cover? — What does the Qur’an actually say?
English: It speaks to men first. Believing men are told to lower their gaze and guard their modesty, and only then are believing women told the same, with one thing added: to draw their head-coverings over their chests and not display their beauty except to the family the verse lists. A second verse tells the Prophet’s ﷺ wives, daughters and the believing women to draw their outer garments about themselves, and gives the reason in its own words: so that they will be known, and not harassed. That is the whole basis, and it is short.

Where it appears: Why do women cover? — What is covered, and does everyone agree?
English: What is covered, and does everyone agree?

Where it appears: Why do women cover? — What is covered, and does everyone agree?
English: The commonly taught form is loose clothing that covers the body and the hair, in front of men outside the immediate family, with the face and hands showing. Whether the face is included is a long-standing difference between scholars, and the page on clothing sets out who says what. A convert usually comes to covering in steps, and that is ordinary, not a failing. No one is entitled to shame a woman for where she is on that road, and the verses above are addressed to her, not to the people watching her.

Where it appears: Why people differ — Do I have to pick one?
English: Do I have to pick one?

Where it appears: Why people differ — Do I have to pick one?
English:
Not on day one, and probably not for a long time. In practice most converts end up following whichever school their mosque follows, which is a perfectly ordinary way to arrive at it and requires no decision at all.

What is worth avoiding is assembling your own from whichever answer is easiest in each case. Not because anybody is policing it, but because that stops being a considered position and becomes a preference wearing a scholar’s name.

Where it appears: Why people differ — Do I have to pick one?
English: If somebody asks which madhhab you follow and you have no answer, "I pray with my local mosque" is a complete one.

Where it appears: Why people differ — How much do they actually disagree about?
English: How much do they actually disagree about?

Where it appears: Why people differ — How much do they actually disagree about?
English:
Far less than the noise suggests. No one differs about the five prayers, the fast of Ramadan, or what is forbidden. The differences are in the detail of practice, such as where the hands rest, whether the intention is said aloud and how many times something is wiped, and in the harder edges of law.

If you learned to pray from this app and prayed behind an imam from any of the four, you would be praying correctly. That is worth knowing before somebody tells you otherwise.

Where it appears: Why people differ — How much do they actually disagree about?
English: That the four schools are all within Sunni Islam, and that following any of them is following Islam, is not itself a matter of dispute.

Where it appears: Why people differ — What is a madhhab?
English: What is a madhhab?

Where it appears: Why people differ — What is a madhhab?
English:
A school of legal reasoning. Four are followed today, Hanafi, Maliki, Shafiʿi and Hanbali, each named after a scholar of the first centuries, and every one of them is Sunni. They are not denominations and not sects. They are four careful attempts at the same question: given the Qur’an and the Sunnah, what exactly follows?

Most Muslims you meet follow one, usually the one their country follows, and most have never thought about it, in the way most people have never thought about the grammar of the language they speak.

Where it appears: Why people differ — Which one does this app teach?
English: Which one does this app teach?

Where it appears: Why people differ — Which one does this app teach?
English:
One clear way, on purpose, because somebody learning to pray needs a path rather than a comparison table. Where a difference is one you will actually meet, at a mosque, from a friend or in a book, the app marks it and says what the other positions are, rather than pretending there is only one.

So when you see a note saying that scholars differ, that is not the app hedging. It is the app telling you in advance about a conversation you are going to have.

Where it appears: Why people differ — Why would there be four answers?
English: Why would there be four answers?

Where it appears: Why people differ — Why would there be four answers?
English:
Because the texts do not spell out every case, and reading them takes judgement. Two scholars can hold the same narration, agree that it is authentic, and still reach different conclusions about what it requires. One reads a command as binding, the other as strongly encouraged. One has a narration the other never received.

That is not a flaw discovered later. It was expected. The Prophet ﷺ said that a judge who strives to reach the right answer is rewarded even when he gets it wrong, and rewarded twice when he gets it right. A religion that rewards a wrong answer reached honestly is a religion that expects careful people to disagree.

Where it appears: Witr — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Witr.

Where it appears: Witr — Is one really enough?
English: Is one really enough?

Where it appears: Witr — Is one really enough?
English: Yes. The Prophet ﷺ named five, three and one, and left the choice to the person praying, so one is a complete witr rather than a shortened version of something else. Most people pray three, and you will see that around you.

Where it appears: Witr — Is one really enough?
English: Start with one. It is the whole prayer, it takes a minute, and it is the version you are least likely to get wrong while you are learning.

Where it appears: Witr — Turn to your left
English: That is Witr complete.

Where it appears: Witr — What if I sleep through it?
English: Pray it before you go to bed. Leaving it to the end of the night is better, but only if you are actually going to be awake. It is meant to be the last thing you pray, not the thing you missed.

Where it appears: Witr — What if I sleep through it?; Fajr — What if I sleep through it?
English: What if I sleep through it?

Where it appears: Witr — Why an odd number?
English: Why an odd number?

Where it appears: Witr — Why an odd number?
English: Because that is what the word means, and it is what you finish the night on.

Where it appears: Work and money — How does Islam see work?
English: How does Islam see work?

Where it appears: Work and money — How does Islam see work?
English: There is no ideal of poverty here. The Prophet ﷺ said nobody has eaten better food than what he earned by his own hands, and noted that the Prophet Dawud ate from his own labour. The Qur’an tells people to disperse and seek God’s bounty as soon as the Friday prayer ends.

Where it appears: Work and money — What about interest?
English: What about interest?

Where it appears: Work and money — What about interest?
English: Riba, usually translated as interest or usury, is prohibited in the Qur’an in strong terms, and the Prophet ﷺ listed consuming it among the gravest sins. In practice this is what makes conventional mortgages, interest-bearing savings and most credit cards a live question for Muslims.

Where it appears: Work and money — What about interest?
English: If you already have a mortgage or a loan, you have not ruined anything, and you do not have to solve it this month. Islamic finance options exist in many countries and vary a great deal. Get advice on your actual situation.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: What if my job touches something forbidden?

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: Directly producing or selling what is prohibited is the clear case. The Prophet ﷺ said the curse on wine falls on ten, its seller and the one who lives off its price among them. What is less clear is indirect involvement: a supermarket cashier who occasionally scans wine, a delivery driver, an accountant at a bank. That distance is exactly what scholars weigh.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: Scholars differ on how much distance from a prohibited thing is enough, so answers vary by how central it is to the job.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: The usual reasoning looks at whether the forbidden thing is the point of the work or incidental to it, at how much of your income depends on it, and at what leaving would cost you. Someone whose whole income comes from selling alcohol is in a different position from someone who occasionally rings it through a till, and someone who cannot simply leave is in a different position again. The clear case is agreed. Where scholars actually differ is on where the line falls, and the line moves with the facts. That is why the answer here is to describe your actual job to someone qualified rather than to read a general rule off a page.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: Do not quit your job the week you become Muslim. Find out what your options are first.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Finish

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: When you are done, say:

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: You are now ready to pray.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: If you are ever rushed or short of water, the four parts the Qur’an itself names are the face, the arms to the elbows, wiping the head, and the feet to the ankles. Once each is enough. Everything else here is the fuller way the Prophet ﷺ did it.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Schools differ over what else is strictly required beyond those four. The intention, keeping to the order, and washing without long pauses in between are each treated as a requirement in some schools and as a recommendation in others. Teaching the full method sidesteps the question entirely, which is why this guide does. Knowing the shorter version matters on the day you have half a bottle of water and a prayer to catch.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: What certainly breaks it: anything that leaves you from the front or the back, such as using the toilet or passing wind, and losing awareness, whether through sleep deep enough that you would not have noticed, fainting, or anything else that takes your senses away.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Bukhari 135 is the Prophet's ﷺ words that the prayer of someone who breaks their wudu is not accepted until they wash again. Abu Huraira, asked what breaking it meant, answered: passing wind. On sleep the wording is "the eyes are the drawstring of the backside, so whoever sleeps should perform wudu". Schools qualify that by how deeply and in what position, but all four agree that heavy sleep ends it. All four also agree that losing your senses another way, whether fainting, anaesthetic or being drunk, ends it too. That is why this note names losing your senses, and not only sleep.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Two more are handled differently by the schools: touching your own private parts, and skin contact with the opposite sex. If one of those happens and you are unsure, washing again takes a minute and settles it.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: The split is not carelessness. It is two authentic narrations pointing different ways. Busrah bint Safwan reports "whoever touches his penis should not pray until he performs wudu"; Talq ibn `Ali reports the Prophet ﷺ answering "is it anything other than a piece of him?" Tirmidhi grades both sound and records that the second is the position of the scholars of Kufa. On the opposite sex, the verse says "or you have touched women", and the argument is over whether that word means intercourse or ordinary contact; `A'isha reports that the Prophet ﷺ kissed her and prayed without washing again.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Neither of the two breaks wudu on its own.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Both break it where there is desire: the private parts touched deliberately with the palm, and contact with the opposite sex accompanied by desire.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Both break it regardless of intention: the private parts touched with the palm and no barrier, and skin contact with an adult of the opposite sex who is not a close relative.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Touching the private parts breaks it; contact with the opposite sex breaks it where there is desire.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Intend in your heart that you are performing wudu to purify yourself for prayer, then say:

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: One wudu covers as many prayers as you like. It lasts until something breaks it, and only then do you wash again.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend; Ghusl — Intend; Tayammum — Intend
English: Intend

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your mouth
English: Rinse your mouth

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your mouth
English: Take water into your mouth with your right hand, swill it around and spit it out. Three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your nose
English: Rinse your nose

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your nose
English: Sniff a little water into your nose with your right hand, then blow it out using your left. Three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your nose
English: Draw it up properly, unless you are fasting, in which case go gently.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your arms
English: Wash your arms

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your arms
English: Wash your right arm from the fingertips to just past the elbow, three times. Then the left, three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your arms
English: Right before left is the pattern for everything that comes in a pair.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your face
English: Wash your face

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your face
English: Wash your whole face three times, from your hairline to under your chin and from ear to ear.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your feet
English: Wash your right foot to just past the ankle, between the toes, three times. Then the left, three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your feet; Ghusl — Wash your feet
English: Wash your feet

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your hands
English: Wash both hands up to the wrists, three times, between the fingers.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your hands; Ghusl — Wash your hands
English: Wash your hands

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your ears
English: Wipe your ears

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your ears
English: With the same wetness, put your index fingers inside your ears and your thumbs behind them, and wipe. Once.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your head
English: Wipe your head

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your head
English: With wet hands, wipe over your head from the front to the back and return to the front. Once.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your head
English: Wiping, not washing, and once rather than three times.

Where it appears: Your children — Do they all get the same?
English: Do they all get the same?

Where it appears: Your children — Do they all get the same?
English: An-Nuʿman’s father gave him a gift and went to have the Prophet ﷺ witness it. He was asked whether he had given every one of his sons the same, and said no. He was told to take it back, and that he would not be made a witness to injustice. A parent’s preference is not treated as a private matter between them and the favoured child. It is named as a wrong done to the others.

Where it appears: Your children — What about discipline?
English: What about discipline?

Where it appears: Your children — What about discipline?
English: Abu Masʿud was beating a boy who served him when he heard a voice behind him. It was the Prophet ﷺ, saying his name. He was told that God has more power over him than he has over the boy. The whip fell out of his hand. Nothing was said about whether the boy deserved it. What was put to him was the size of his own position, which had been the whole basis of the beating.

Where it appears: Your children — What is owed to a daughter?
English: What is owed to a daughter?

Where it appears: Your children — What is owed to a daughter?
English: A woman came to ʿAisha with two daughters, asking for anything. She was given a single date, and she split it between the two girls and ate none of it herself. When the Prophet ﷺ was told, he said that whoever is given the care of daughters and treats them well will have them as a protection from the Fire. The context matters. This was said in a place where a daughter was widely counted as a disappointment.

Where it appears: Your children — What is owed to a daughter?
English: The Qur’an addresses the same attitude directly, and says that God gives daughters to whom He wills and sons to whom He wills, in that order.

Where it appears: Your children — Where does it start?
English: Where does it start?

Where it appears: Your children — Where does it start?
English: A man watched the Prophet ﷺ kiss his grandson and said that he had ten children and had never kissed one of them. He was not praised for it. He was told that whoever shows no mercy is shown none. Affection towards a child is not treated here as a soft extra on top of raising them. It is the thing being asked for, and its absence was worth correcting on the spot.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What do I do when I walk in?
English: What do I do when I walk in?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What do I do when I walk in?
English: There will be a shoe rack by the door. Take your shoes off there and carry them in if the rack is full. Step in with your right foot. There are usually separate entrances or areas for men and women. Look for the signs, or ask; nobody minds being asked.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens afterwards?
English: What happens afterwards?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens afterwards?
English: People turn and greet whoever is beside them. Say salam back. Someone will very likely ask if you are new. This is the moment the whole trip is actually for, and it is worth staying ten minutes for it.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens in the prayer?
English: What happens in the prayer?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens in the prayer?
English: People stand shoulder to shoulder in straight lines, filling from the front. Stand in a line, follow the imam, and do what the row does. You do not say anything aloud and nobody is watching you.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What if I get something wrong?
English: What if I get something wrong?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What if I get something wrong?
English: All of these are fine: being a beat behind in the movements, not knowing where to stand, your phone going off, asking a stranger what to do, leaving straight afterwards, getting the words wrong under your breath.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What if I get something wrong?
English: Everyone in that room was new once, including the imam. No one is grading you, and the people who notice you are new are almost always pleased about it.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What should I do before I go?
English: What should I do before I go?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What should I do before I go?
English: Do your wudu at home if you can. It is one less thing to work out when you arrive. Wear clean clothes that cover you from the navel to the knees at minimum; loose trousers and a long top are entirely normal. What a woman covers is no different here from anywhere else in front of men outside the family, and the clothing guide sets it out with the verses behind it.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — When should I go the first time?
English: When should I go the first time?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — When should I go the first time?
English: Friday midday is the busiest hour of the week. For a first visit, go for a normal prayer: Dhuhr in the early afternoon, or ʿIsha at night. Fewer people, more room to watch what everyone else does.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — When should I go the first time?
English: Friday prayer is obligatory for men, so you will need to go eventually. It is easier once the building is already familiar.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — Where do I sit?
English: Where do I sit?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — Where do I sit?
English: Pray two short rakʿahs before you sit down. It is what everyone does on entering. Then sit anywhere on the carpet. There is no reserved seating and no collection.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — Where do I sit?
English: If a prayer is already in progress, join the line where you are and follow the imam from wherever he has got to. When he finishes and gives salam, stand back up and pray the rakʿahs you missed on your own. That is what completes your prayer.

Where it appears: Your mother, three times — What does it actually look like?
English: What does it actually look like?

Where it appears: Your mother, three times — What does it actually look like?
English: The Qur’an sets the bar at a syllable. It says that if one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them so much as "uff", the sound of being irritated, and do not push them away, but speak to them a noble word. Then it goes further and asks for the wing of humility to be lowered to them out of mercy. Nothing about that is about grand gestures. It is about tone of voice on a bad day.

Where it appears: Your mother, three times — What does it actually look like?
English: The command sits directly after the command to worship God alone, in the same sentence. That placement is the point being made.

Where it appears: Your mother, three times — What if they ask me to do something wrong?
English: What if they ask me to do something wrong?

Where it appears: Your mother, three times — What if they ask me to do something wrong?
English: There is a limit, and the Qur’an states it while keeping everything else in place. If they press you to associate anything with God, do not obey them in that. The verse that says so still calls for goodness to them, and elsewhere the same instruction adds that you keep company with them in this world in a good way. So the refusal is narrow. It covers the thing being asked, not the relationship.

Where it appears: Your mother, three times — What if they ask me to do something wrong?
English: If your parents are not Muslim, or do not know yet, the family page answers those questions rather than this one.

Where it appears: Your mother, three times — Who deserves the most from me?
English: Who deserves the most from me?

Where it appears: Your mother, three times — Who deserves the most from me?
English: A man asked the Prophet ﷺ exactly that. He was told his mother. He asked who came next, and was told his mother. He asked again, and was told his mother a third time. Only on the fourth asking was he told his father. The repetition is the teaching. It was not a slip, and the man kept asking because he did not expect the same answer twice.

Where it appears: Your mother, three times — Why the mother three times?
English: Why the mother three times?

Where it appears: Your mother, three times — Why the mother three times?
English: The Qur’an answers it in the places where it commands kindness to parents. It says his mother carried him in weakness upon weakness. It says she carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship. The father is commanded in the same breath, and the mother is described. What she is owed is not a sentiment. It is a debt for something already done that cannot be repaid.

Where it appears: Your neighbour — How much does a neighbour matter?
English: How much does a neighbour matter?

Where it appears: Your neighbour — How much does a neighbour matter?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said that Jibril kept on urging him about the neighbour until he thought the neighbour would be given a share of the inheritance. That is the measure being offered. Not a general encouragement to be pleasant, but a pressure so persistent that the man receiving it expected a legal right to come out of it.

Where it appears: Your neighbour — What is the floor?
English: What is the floor?

Where it appears: Your neighbour — What is the floor?
English: That they are safe from you. The Prophet ﷺ said that a person whose neighbour is not secure from his harm will not enter Paradise. Before any question of gifts or visits, the first thing owed to the person on the other side of the wall is that living next to you costs them nothing.

Where it appears: Your neighbour — Which neighbour, and how far?
English: Which neighbour, and how far?

Where it appears: Your neighbour — Which neighbour, and how far?
English: ʿAisha asked which of two neighbours she should give to. She was told the one whose door is nearer. The Qur’an lists both, the near neighbour and the one further off, in a verse that runs through everyone with a claim on you, from parents down to the traveller and the companion at your side. So the circle is wide, and nearness decides the order rather than the obligation.

Where it appears: Your neighbour — Which neighbour, and how far?
English: Nothing in these texts asks what religion the neighbour is, and the page does not add the question.

Where it appears: ʿAsr — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying ʿAsr.

Where it appears: ʿAsr — Turn to your left
English: That is ʿAsr complete.

Where it appears: ʿAsr — What is ʿAsr?
English: What is ʿAsr?

Where it appears: ʿAsr — What is ʿAsr?
English: Four silent rakʿahs in the last stretch of the afternoon, prayed while the day is still busy. That is exactly why so much was said about it.

Where it appears: ʿAsr — Why does it matter so much?
English: Four narrations give this one afternoon prayer unusual weight.

Where it appears: ʿIsha — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying ʿIsha.

Where it appears: ʿIsha — Is it hard to end the day with it?
English: Is it hard to end the day with it?

Where it appears: ʿIsha — Is it hard to end the day with it?
English: It is the easy one to skip, and the Prophet ﷺ said exactly that. No prayer sits heavier on a hypocrite than ʿIsha and Fajr, and if people knew what was in them they would come even if they had to crawl. Praying it is a quiet decision about how the day ends.

Where it appears: ʿIsha — Turn to your left
English: That is ʿIsha complete.

Where it appears: ʿIsha — What is ʿIsha?
English: What is ʿIsha?

Where it appears: ʿIsha — What is ʿIsha?
English: Four rakʿahs, prayed once night has settled. Prayed in congregation, it is counted like standing half the night in prayer.
